Acute liver failure and drug-induced liver injury
Acute asthma and COPD exacerbation in the ED
Vascular Emergencies: AAA and Acute Limb Ischemia

en-cardio.q: What are the ECG criteria for STEMI in leads V2–V3 (men ≥40 years)?
en-cardio.a: New ST elevation at the J point **≥2 mm in V2–V3** (≥2.5 mm in men <40; ≥1.5 mm in women), and ≥1 mm in other contiguous leads, per the Fourth Universal Definition of MI.

en-cardio.q: What defines myocardial infarction under the Fourth Universal Definition?
en-cardio.a: A **rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin** with at least one value above the 99th percentile URL, plus clinical evidence of ischemia (symptoms, new ECG changes, new Q waves, imaging loss of viable myocardium, or intracoronary thrombus).

en-cardio.q: What is the preferred reperfusion strategy for STEMI, and the time target?
en-cardio.a: **Primary PCI** if achievable within 120 minutes of diagnosis (ESC); ACC/AHA target first medical contact-to-device ≤90 min. If PCI cannot be done in time, give fibrinolysis within 10 min of diagnosis (no contraindications).

en-cardio.q: What is the typical dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) after ACS and its default duration?
en-cardio.a: **Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor** (ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel in ACS) for **12 months** by default; shorter courses are considered when bleeding risk is high.

en-cardio.q: Name absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis.
en-cardio.a: Prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 3–6 months, CNS neoplasm or AV malformation, recent major trauma/surgery/head injury (≤1 month), active bleeding, aortic dissection, and non-compressible punctures in past 24 h.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves in a patient with chest pain suggests what?
en-cardio.a: **Posterior MI** (usually left circumflex or RCA occlusion). Confirm with posterior leads V7–V9 showing ST elevation ≥0.5 mm; manage as STEMI equivalent.

en-cardio.q: Which drug should be avoided in inferior MI with right ventricular involvement and why?
en-cardio.a: **Nitrates** (and other preload reducers such as diuretics): RV infarction is preload dependent, so they can cause profound hypotension. Check V4R for ST elevation; treat hypotension with IV fluids.

en-cardio.q: What are the mechanical complications of MI and when do they typically occur?
en-cardio.a: **Papillary muscle rupture** (acute MR), **ventricular septal rupture**, and **free wall rupture** (tamponade), classically 3–7 days post-MI; less common with early reperfusion. LV aneurysm and thrombus occur later.

en-cardio.q: How is heart failure classified by left ventricular ejection fraction?
en-cardio.a: **HFrEF** LVEF ≤40%, **HFmrEF** 41–49%, **HFpEF** ≥50% (with structural/functional abnormality and raised natriuretic peptides). HFimpEF: previously ≤40% now >40%.

en-cardio.q: What are the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy in HFrEF?
en-cardio.a: **ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACEI/ARB**, **evidence-based beta-blocker** (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), **mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist**, and **SGLT2 inhibitor** (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin). All reduce mortality/HF hospitalization.

en-cardio.q: Which natriuretic peptide thresholds make heart failure unlikely in the non-acute setting?
en-cardio.a: **NT-proBNP <125 pg/mL** or **BNP <35 pg/mL** (ESC). In acute presentations, cut-offs are higher: NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL or BNP <100 pg/mL.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: why must sacubitril/valsartan not be started within 36 hours of an ACE inhibitor?
en-cardio.a: Combined neprilysin and ACE inhibition markedly increases **angioedema** risk from bradykinin accumulation. A 36-hour washout is required when switching from an ACEI.

en-cardio.q: Which drug class improves symptoms and mortality in HFpEF according to recent trials?
en-cardio.a: **SGLT2 inhibitors** (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) reduce HF hospitalization/CV death in HFmrEF/HFpEF; diuretics treat congestion. Finerenone showed benefit in HFmrEF/HFpEF (FINEARTS-HF).

en-cardio.q: What are the indications for an ICD for primary prevention in heart failure?
en-cardio.a: Symptomatic HF (NYHA II–III) with **LVEF ≤35%** despite ≥3 months of optimal medical therapy and expected survival >1 year; evidence strongest in ischemic cardiomyopathy.

en-cardio.q: When is cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) indicated?
en-cardio.a: Symptomatic HFrEF with **LVEF ≤35%**, sinus rhythm, and **QRS ≥150 ms with LBBB morphology** (strongest indication) despite optimal medical therapy; also considered for QRS 130–149 ms LBBB.

en-cardio.q: What is the initial management of acute decompensated heart failure with congestion?
en-cardio.a: **IV loop diuretic** (e.g., furosemide IV at 1–2.5 times the oral daily dose, or 20–40 mg if diuretic-naive), oxygen if SpO2 <90%, vasodilators if hypertensive, and non-invasive ventilation for respiratory distress/pulmonary edema.

en-cardio.q: How is the CHA2DS2-VASc score calculated?
en-cardio.a: **C**HF 1, **H**ypertension 1, **A**ge ≥75 2, **D**iabetes 1, **S**troke/TIA/thromboembolism 2, **V**ascular disease 1, **A**ge 65–74 1, **S**ex category female 1. The 2024 ESC guideline uses CHA2DS2-VA (sex removed).

en-cardio.q: When is oral anticoagulation recommended in non-valvular AF?
en-cardio.a: ESC 2024: recommended at CHA2DS2-VA ≥2, considered at 1. ACC/AHA 2023: recommended at annual stroke risk ≥2% (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 men, ≥3 women). **DOACs are preferred over warfarin**.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: which AF patients must receive warfarin rather than a DOAC?
en-cardio.a: Patients with **mechanical heart valves** or **moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis** (valvular AF). DOACs are contraindicated or unproven in these groups.

en-cardio.q: What is the initial management of AF with rapid ventricular response and hemodynamic instability?
en-cardio.a: **Emergency synchronized electrical cardioversion**. Instability includes hypotension, shock, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure, or syncope.

en-cardio.q: Which rate-control agents are used in AF and which is preferred with reduced ejection fraction?
en-cardio.a: Beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil), and digoxin. In **LVEF ≤40%, avoid diltiazem/verapamil**; use beta-blockers and/or digoxin.

en-cardio.q: What is the rule for cardioversion in AF of uncertain or ≥48 hours duration?
en-cardio.a: Requires **≥3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation** before or **TEE excluding left atrial thrombus**, and anticoagulation for **at least 4 weeks** afterwards (ESC recent guidance advises a lower 24-hour threshold in high-risk patients).

en-cardio.q: Which patients with AF benefit from early catheter ablation?
en-cardio.a: Symptomatic paroxysmal AF (first-line option), drug-refractory AF, and **HFrEF with AF** where ablation reduces mortality and HF hospitalization (CASTLE-AF). EAST-AFNET 4 supports early rhythm control.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: what drug class is dangerous in AF with pre-excitation (WPW)?
en-cardio.a: **AV nodal blockers** (adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin) can accelerate accessory pathway conduction and precipitate VF. Use synchronized cardioversion or procainamide/ibutilide.

en-cardio.q: How do ACC/AHA and ESC define hypertension by office blood pressure?
en-cardio.a: **ACC/AHA 2017**: ≥130/80 mmHg (stage 1). **ESC 2018/NICE**: ≥140/90 mmHg. ESC 2024 adds an 'elevated BP' category 120–139/70–89 mmHg.

en-cardio.q: What are first-line antihypertensive drug classes for most patients?
en-cardio.a: **ACE inhibitor or ARB, dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic**. ESC recommends starting most patients on a single-pill two-drug combination.

en-cardio.q: What defines resistant hypertension and the preferred fourth-line drug?
en-cardio.a: BP above target despite **three drugs at optimal doses, including a diuretic**, after excluding pseudoresistance (adherence, technique, white-coat). Fourth-line: **spironolactone** (PATHWAY-2).

en-cardio.q: What distinguishes hypertensive emergency from urgency?
en-cardio.a: **Emergency**: severe BP elevation with **acute target-organ damage** (encephalopathy, stroke, ACS, acute pulmonary edema, aortic dissection, AKI, eclampsia). Urgency lacks acute organ damage and is managed orally.

en-cardio.q: How fast should BP be lowered in a hypertensive emergency (without dissection or stroke)?
en-cardio.a: Reduce mean arterial pressure by **no more than 25% in the first hour**, then to 160/100–110 mmHg over 2–6 h, then normal over 24–48 h. Aortic dissection: SBP <120 mmHg within the first hour.

en-cardio.q: Name clinical clues suggesting secondary hypertension.
en-cardio.a: Onset <30 years, resistant or sudden worsening hypertension, hypokalemia (**primary aldosteronism**), paroxysmal symptoms (pheochromocytoma), renal bruit or creatinine rise on ACEI (renovascular), snoring (OSA), and radio-femoral delay (coarctation).

en-cardio.q: What is the most common cause of secondary hypertension that is often missed?
en-cardio.a: **Primary aldosteronism** (5–10% of hypertensives, more in resistant HTN). Screen with the **aldosterone-to-renin ratio**; hypokalemia is present in only a minority.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: which antihypertensives are contraindicated in pregnancy and which are preferred?
en-cardio.a: **ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and direct renin inhibitors are contraindicated** (fetotoxic). Preferred: **labetalol, nifedipine (extended release), methyldopa**.

en-cardio.q: What echocardiographic criteria define severe aortic stenosis?
en-cardio.a: **Aortic valve area <1.0 cm²**, **mean gradient ≥40 mmHg**, and **peak velocity ≥4.0 m/s**. Low-flow low-gradient AS may need dobutamine echo or CT calcium scoring.

en-cardio.q: What is the classic triad of symptoms in aortic stenosis?
en-cardio.a: **Angina, syncope (exertional), and dyspnea/heart failure**. Symptom onset marks a steep rise in mortality and is an indication for valve replacement.

en-cardio.q: How do you choose between TAVI and SAVR for severe aortic stenosis?
en-cardio.a: Heart Team decision. ESC 2021: TAVI favored at **age ≥75** or high surgical risk; SAVR for younger, low-risk patients. ACC/AHA 2020 uses age thresholds of 65–80 for shared decision-making.

en-cardio.q: What murmur is heard in mitral regurgitation and where does it radiate?
en-cardio.a: **Holosystolic (pansystolic) blowing murmur** at the apex radiating to the **axilla**. Chronic primary MR is repaired when symptomatic or with LVEF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm.

en-cardio.q: What are the auscultatory features of mitral stenosis?
en-cardio.a: **Loud S1, opening snap, and low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble** at the apex (best in left lateral decubitus with the bell), with presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm. Most cases are rheumatic.

en-cardio.q: What is first-line intervention for symptomatic severe rheumatic mitral stenosis?
en-cardio.a: **Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy** if valve anatomy is favorable and there is no left atrial thrombus or more than mild MR; otherwise surgical valve replacement.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: which murmur increases with Valsalva and standing?
en-cardio.a: **Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy** (and mitral valve prolapse click moves earlier). Most other murmurs, including aortic stenosis, decrease with reduced preload.

en-cardio.q: What are the signs of chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
en-cardio.a: **Early diastolic decrescendo murmur** at left sternal border, wide pulse pressure, collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, Corrigan, de Musset, and Quincke signs; Austin Flint mid-diastolic rumble may be present.

en-cardio.q: What are the major Duke criteria for infective endocarditis?
en-cardio.a: **Microbiological**: typical organisms in ≥2 separate blood cultures (or persistently positive), or Coxiella burnetii serology. **Imaging**: echo evidence of vegetation, abscess, new valvular regurgitation or prosthetic dehiscence (PET/CT and cardiac CT added in 2023 criteria).

en-cardio.q: How many blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics in suspected endocarditis?
en-cardio.a: **Three sets** from separate venipunctures, before antibiotics, ideally spaced (at least 30 minutes apart in stable patients) to document continuous bacteremia.

en-cardio.q: What is the most common organism in infective endocarditis overall and in IV drug users?
en-cardio.a: **Staphylococcus aureus** is the most common overall in high-income countries. In people who inject drugs it typically affects the **tricuspid valve** (right-sided IE with septic pulmonary emboli).

en-cardio.q: Which organism in endocarditis should prompt colonoscopy?
en-cardio.a: **Streptococcus gallolyticus** (formerly S. bovis biotype I) — strongly associated with **colorectal neoplasia**.

en-cardio.q: What are the main indications for early surgery in infective endocarditis?
en-cardio.a: **Heart failure** from valve dysfunction, **uncontrolled infection** (abscess, fistula, persistent bacteremia, fungal or resistant organism), and **prevention of embolism** (large vegetation >10 mm with embolic event, or very large >30 mm).

en-cardio.q: Who should receive antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures?
en-cardio.a: High-risk patients only: **prosthetic valves or valve repair material**, **previous endocarditis**, and certain congenital heart disease (unrepaired cyanotic, or repaired with residual defects/within 6 months). NICE does not routinely recommend prophylaxis.

en-cardio.q: What are the classic peripheral stigmata of endocarditis?
en-cardio.a: **Splinter hemorrhages**, **Janeway lesions** (painless palmar/plantar macules, embolic), **Osler nodes** (painful finger pulp nodules, immunologic), **Roth spots** (retinal), plus clubbing and splenomegaly in subacute disease.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: why is TTE alone insufficient in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis?
en-cardio.a: **TTE has low sensitivity** for prosthetic valves and perivalvular abscess; **TEE is required**, and PET/CT is useful when echo is inconclusive.

en-cardio.q: What are the diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis?
en-cardio.a: At least **2 of 4**: pleuritic chest pain (relieved by sitting forward), **pericardial friction rub**, **widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression**, and new or worsening pericardial effusion.

en-cardio.q: What is first-line treatment for acute idiopathic pericarditis?
en-cardio.a: **High-dose aspirin or NSAID** (e.g., ibuprofen 600 mg orally every 8 h) plus **colchicine 0.5 mg once or twice daily (weight-based) for 3 months**, with gastroprotection. Colchicine halves recurrence.

en-cardio.q: What is Beck's triad and what does it indicate?
en-cardio.a: **Hypotension, raised JVP, and muffled heart sounds** — indicates **cardiac tamponade**.

en-cardio.q: What is pulsus paradoxus?
en-cardio.a: An **inspiratory fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg**, classic in cardiac tamponade; also seen in severe asthma/COPD exacerbation and massive PE.

en-cardio.q: What are the ECG findings in large pericardial effusion or tamponade?
en-cardio.a: **Low QRS voltage** and **electrical alternans** (beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation from the heart swinging), often with sinus tachycardia.

en-cardio.q: What is the definitive management of cardiac tamponade?
en-cardio.a: Urgent **pericardiocentesis** (echo-guided) or surgical drainage. Avoid diuretics and vasodilators; IV fluids may temporize while drainage is arranged.

en-cardio.q: Which features predict poor prognosis in acute pericarditis and warrant admission?
en-cardio.a: **Fever >38 °C**, subacute onset, large effusion or tamponade, **failure to respond to NSAIDs after 1 week**, myopericarditis, immunosuppression, trauma, or oral anticoagulation.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: how do you differentiate constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy?
en-cardio.a: Constriction shows **ventricular interdependence** (respiratory septal shift), pericardial thickening/calcification, pericardial knock, **Kussmaul sign**, and normal/near-normal BNP. Restriction shows markedly elevated BNP and reduced tissue Doppler e′ velocities.

en-cardio.q: How is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy defined in adults?
en-cardio.a: **LV wall thickness ≥15 mm** in any segment not explained by loading conditions (≥13 mm in first-degree relatives of an affected individual). Commonly due to sarcomeric gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3), autosomal dominant.

en-cardio.q: What is first-line therapy for symptomatic obstructive HCM?
en-cardio.a: **Non-vasodilating beta-blockers** (or verapamil/diltiazem if intolerant). **Mavacamten** (cardiac myosin inhibitor) is an option for persistent symptoms; septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation for refractory cases.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: which drugs worsen LV outflow tract obstruction in HCM?
en-cardio.a: **Vasodilators** (nitrates, dihydropyridines, ACEI), **diuretics at high dose**, **positive inotropes**, and dehydration — all reduce preload/afterload and increase obstruction.

en-cardio.q: What are major risk factors for sudden cardiac death in HCM?
en-cardio.a: Family history of SCD, unexplained syncope, **maximal wall thickness ≥30 mm**, non-sustained VT, LV apical aneurysm, extensive LGE on MRI, and LVEF <50%. ESC uses the HCM Risk-SCD calculator.

en-cardio.q: What are common causes of dilated cardiomyopathy?
en-cardio.a: **Genetic** (e.g., TTN truncation, LMNA), **alcohol**, myocarditis (viral), **cardiotoxic chemotherapy** (anthracyclines, trastuzumab), peripartum, tachycardia-induced, and thyroid disease. Ischemic heart disease must be excluded.

en-cardio.q: Which cardiomyopathy presents with ventricular arrhythmias and epsilon waves?
en-cardio.a: **Arrhythmogenic (right ventricular) cardiomyopathy**: fibrofatty replacement, T-wave inversion in V1–V3, epsilon waves, and LBBB-morphology VT; desmosomal gene mutations. Avoid competitive endurance exercise.

en-cardio.q: What clinical clues suggest cardiac amyloidosis?
en-cardio.a: HFpEF with increased wall thickness but **low ECG voltage**, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, apical sparing on strain echo, and troponin elevation. Diagnose ATTR with **bone scintigraphy plus exclusion of monoclonal protein**.

en-cardio.q: What defines peripartum cardiomyopathy?
en-cardio.a: **LVEF <45%** heart failure arising toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery without another cause. Bromocriptine may be considered (ESC); ACEI/ARB/ARNI contraindicated during pregnancy.

en-cardio.q: What is syncope?
en-cardio.a: **Transient loss of consciousness due to cerebral hypoperfusion**, with rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery.

en-cardio.q: What is the most common cause of syncope?
en-cardio.a: **Reflex (vasovagal) syncope** — triggered by prolonged standing, pain, emotion, or heat, with prodrome of nausea, sweating, and pallor.

en-cardio.q: Which features suggest cardiac syncope (high-risk)?
en-cardio.a: Syncope **during exertion or supine**, sudden palpitations before, no prodrome, known structural heart disease or low LVEF, family history of sudden death, and abnormal ECG (e.g., Mobitz II, bifascicular block, long QT, Brugada).

en-cardio.q: How is orthostatic hypotension defined?
en-cardio.a: Sustained **fall in SBP ≥20 mmHg or DBP ≥10 mmHg** within 3 minutes of standing (or SBP <90 mmHg). Classic causes: volume depletion, drugs, autonomic failure.

en-cardio.q: What initial evaluation is mandatory in every patient with syncope?
en-cardio.a: **Careful history, physical examination including orthostatic BP, and a 12-lead ECG**; further tests are guided by risk stratification.

en-cardio.q: Which ECG findings suggest arrhythmic syncope?
en-cardio.a: **Mobitz II or complete heart block**, sinus pauses >3 s, bifascicular block, **pre-excitation**, **prolonged or short QT**, **Brugada type 1 pattern**, epsilon waves, and pathological Q waves.

en-cardio.q: What investigation suits recurrent unexplained syncope with infrequent episodes?
en-cardio.a: **Implantable loop recorder** — superior diagnostic yield for infrequent episodes compared with Holter monitoring.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: how do you distinguish syncope from a seizure clinically?
en-cardio.a: Seizures suggest by **tongue biting (lateral)**, prolonged post-ictal confusion, head turning, and cyanosis. Brief myoclonic jerks and incontinence can occur in syncope and do not confirm seizure.

en-cardio.q: What LDL-C targets does the ESC recommend by risk category?
en-cardio.a: **Very high risk**: <55 mg/dL (<1.4 mmol/L) and ≥50% reduction; **high risk**: <70 mg/dL (<1.8 mmol/L); **moderate**: <100 mg/dL (<2.6 mmol/L). ACC/AHA uses LDL thresholds (e.g., 70 mg/dL) to add non-statin therapy.

en-cardio.q: What is first-line lipid-lowering therapy after ACS?
en-cardio.a: **High-intensity statin** (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg orally daily). Add **ezetimibe** then a **PCSK9 inhibitor** if LDL targets are not met.

en-cardio.q: What is the mechanism of statins?
en-cardio.a: Inhibition of **HMG-CoA reductase**, the rate-limiting step in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, which upregulates hepatic LDL receptors and increases LDL clearance.

en-cardio.q: What are key statin adverse effects and when to stop?
en-cardio.a: **Myalgia** (common), rarely **myopathy/rhabdomyolysis**; asymptomatic transaminase rise. Stop if **CK >10 times ULN** or severe symptoms; small increase in new-onset diabetes.

en-cardio.q: When should familial hypercholesterolemia be suspected?
en-cardio.a: **LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL (≥4.9 mmol/L)** in adults, tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus <45 years, or premature ASCVD in the patient or first-degree relatives. Use Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria; cascade-screen relatives.

en-cardio.q: Is aspirin recommended for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease?
en-cardio.a: **Not routinely.** Bleeding risk offsets modest benefit; ACC/AHA allows consideration in selected adults 40–70 at high risk and low bleeding risk. It is indicated for secondary prevention.

en-cardio.q: What does lipoprotein(a) represent and when should it be measured?
en-cardio.a: A genetically determined, **independent causal ASCVD risk factor**. ESC recommends measuring it **at least once in every adult's lifetime**; levels >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) confer risk similar to heterozygous FH.

en-cardio.q: Exam trap: which statins interact with clarithromycin and grapefruit?
en-cardio.a: **Simvastatin, lovastatin, and atorvastatin** (CYP3A4-metabolized) — risk of myopathy. Rosuvastatin and pravastatin are less affected.

en-pulmo.q: What lung function findings support an asthma diagnosis?
en-pulmo.a: **Variable expiratory airflow limitation**: FEV1/FVC reduced plus **bronchodilator reversibility** (FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL), or excessive PEF variability, or positive bronchial challenge. FeNO supports type 2 inflammation.

en-pulmo.q: Why does GINA no longer recommend SABA-only treatment in adults?
en-pulmo.a: SABA-only therapy is associated with increased **exacerbations and asthma death**. GINA recommends **ICS-containing treatment** for all adults, preferably as-needed low-dose **ICS-formoterol** (Track 1).

en-pulmo.q: What is maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)?
en-pulmo.a: Using a single **ICS-formoterol inhaler** (budesonide-formoterol or beclometasone-formoterol) both daily and as needed; reduces severe exacerbations versus fixed-dose ICS-LABA with SABA reliever.

en-pulmo.q: What features define a life-threatening asthma attack (BTS)?
en-pulmo.a: **PEF <33% predicted**, SpO2 <92%, **PaO2 <8 kPa**, **normal or rising PaCO2** (4.6–6.0 kPa), silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, arrhythmia, exhaustion, altered consciousness, or hypotension.

en-pulmo.q: What is initial management of acute severe asthma in adults?
en-pulmo.a: **Oxygen** to SpO2 93–95%, **nebulized salbutamol 5 mg** (repeat or back-to-back), **ipratropium 0.5 mg** nebulized, and **systemic corticosteroid** (prednisolone 40–50 mg orally or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 h). Consider IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: why is a normal PaCO2 worrying in acute asthma?
en-pulmo.a: Patients normally hyperventilate and are **hypocapnic**; a normal or rising PaCO2 signals **fatigue and impending respiratory failure** — a life-threatening feature requiring ICU review.

en-pulmo.q: Which biologics are used in severe eosinophilic asthma?
en-pulmo.a: **Anti-IL-5** (mepolizumab, reslizumab), **anti-IL-5R** (benralizumab), **anti-IL-4Rα** (dupilumab), and **anti-TSLP** (tezepelumab); **anti-IgE** (omalizumab) for allergic asthma.

en-pulmo.q: Which drug classes can worsen asthma?
en-pulmo.a: **Non-selective beta-blockers** (including eye drops), and **NSAIDs/aspirin** in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (triad: asthma, nasal polyps, NSAID sensitivity).

en-pulmo.q: How is COPD diagnosed on spirometry?
en-pulmo.a: **Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70** in a patient with compatible symptoms and exposure (smoking, biomass). Severity by FEV1 % predicted (GOLD 1–4).

en-pulmo.q: How does GOLD group patients for initial pharmacologic therapy?
en-pulmo.a: **ABE tool**: Group A (few symptoms, low risk) — a bronchodilator; **Group B** (mMRC ≥2 or CAT ≥10) — **LABA+LAMA**; **Group E** (≥2 moderate or ≥1 hospitalized exacerbation) — LABA+LAMA, adding ICS if eosinophils ≥300/µL.

en-pulmo.q: Which interventions improve survival in COPD?
en-pulmo.a: **Smoking cessation**, **long-term oxygen therapy** in chronic severe hypoxemia, **pulmonary rehabilitation** after exacerbation, lung volume reduction in selected patients, and triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA) in frequent exacerbators.

en-pulmo.q: What are the criteria for long-term oxygen therapy in COPD?
en-pulmo.a: **PaO2 ≤7.3 kPa (55 mmHg) or SaO2 ≤88%**, or PaO2 7.3–8.0 kPa (55–60 mmHg) with polycythemia, pulmonary hypertension, or cor pulmonale; confirmed twice over 3 weeks when stable, used ≥15 h/day.

en-pulmo.q: What is the standard treatment of an acute COPD exacerbation?
en-pulmo.a: **Short-acting bronchodilators**, **prednisolone 40 mg orally daily for 5 days**, **antibiotics** if increased sputum purulence (or ventilation needed), and **controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 88–92%**.

en-pulmo.q: When is non-invasive ventilation indicated in COPD exacerbation?
en-pulmo.a: **Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis**: pH ≤7.35 and PaCO2 >6.0 kPa (45 mmHg) persisting despite optimal medical therapy. NIV reduces intubation and mortality.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: why target SpO2 88–92% in COPD patients at risk of hypercapnia?
en-pulmo.a: High-flow oxygen worsens **V/Q mismatch** and the Haldane effect (hypoxic drive loss plays a smaller role), causing **hypercapnic acidosis**. Use Venturi masks and check ABG.

en-pulmo.q: Which condition should be screened for in young patients with emphysema?
en-pulmo.a: **Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency** — panlobular, lower-zone emphysema, often with liver disease. WHO recommends testing all patients with COPD once.

en-pulmo.q: What is the CURB-65 score?
en-pulmo.a: **C**onfusion, **U**rea >7 mmol/L, **R**espiratory rate ≥30, **B**P systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60, age ≥**65**. Score 0–1 home, 2 consider hospital, 3–5 severe (consider ICU).

en-pulmo.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
en-pulmo.a: **Streptococcus pneumoniae**. Other causes: Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella, Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza), and respiratory viruses.

en-pulmo.q: What is empirical therapy for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia in adults (BTS/NICE)?
en-pulmo.a: **Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 5 days**; doxycycline or clarithromycin if penicillin allergic. ATS/IDSA (US): amoxicillin, doxycycline, or a macrolide if local resistance <25% in healthy adults.

en-pulmo.q: What is empirical therapy for severe CAP in hospitalized adults?
en-pulmo.a: **Beta-lactam plus macrolide** (e.g., ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; BTS: co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin), or a respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy. Add MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage only with risk factors.

en-pulmo.q: What defines hospital-acquired pneumonia?
en-pulmo.a: Pneumonia occurring **≥48 hours after admission** not incubating at admission; ventilator-associated pneumonia is ≥48 h after intubation. Cover Pseudomonas and MRSA based on local risk.

en-pulmo.q: Which clues suggest Legionella pneumonia?
en-pulmo.a: **Hyponatremia**, deranged LFTs, diarrhea, confusion, high fever, and exposure to air-conditioning/water systems. Diagnose with **urinary antigen** (detects serogroup 1).

en-pulmo.q: When should follow-up chest X-ray be performed after pneumonia?
en-pulmo.a: BTS: at around **6 weeks** in patients with persistent symptoms or signs, or at higher risk of malignancy (e.g., smokers, age >50).

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: which pneumonia classically follows influenza with cavitation?
en-pulmo.a: **Staphylococcus aureus** (including PVL-producing strains) — rapid, necrotizing, cavitating pneumonia; also causes pneumatoceles in children.

en-pulmo.q: How is D-dimer used in suspected PE?
en-pulmo.a: Only in **low or intermediate (PE unlikely)** pretest probability: a negative D-dimer excludes PE. Age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 µg/L above 50) improves specificity. Do not use in high probability.

en-pulmo.q: What are the PERC rule criteria?
en-pulmo.a: In low pretest probability, PE can be excluded if all: **age <50, HR <100, SpO2 ≥95%**, no hemoptysis, no estrogen use, no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no recent surgery/trauma.

en-pulmo.q: What is first-line imaging for suspected PE?
en-pulmo.a: **CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)**. V/Q scanning is preferred when contrast is contraindicated or radiation must be minimized (e.g., pregnancy with normal CXR).

en-pulmo.q: What defines high-risk (massive) PE?
en-pulmo.a: PE with **hemodynamic instability**: cardiac arrest, obstructive shock, or persistent hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min) not due to other causes.

en-pulmo.q: What is the treatment of high-risk PE?
en-pulmo.a: **Systemic thrombolysis** (e.g., alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 h) with unfractionated heparin; surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy if thrombolysis contraindicated or fails.

en-pulmo.q: What is the first-line anticoagulant for most patients with PE?
en-pulmo.a: A **DOAC** (apixaban, rivaroxaban, or edoxaban/dabigatran after parenteral lead-in). Avoid DOACs in severe renal impairment, antiphospholipid syndrome, and pregnancy (use LMWH).

en-pulmo.q: How long should anticoagulation be given after a PE?
en-pulmo.a: At least **3 months**. Stop after provoked PE with a major transient risk factor; consider **indefinite anticoagulation** for unprovoked PE, recurrent VTE, or persistent risk factors (e.g., active cancer).

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: what is the most common ECG finding in PE?
en-pulmo.a: **Sinus tachycardia**. The S1Q3T3 pattern is classic but uncommon; right heart strain signs include RBBB, right axis deviation, and T-wave inversion in V1–V4.

en-pulmo.q: What are the typical clinical features of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
en-pulmo.a: Older (usually >60), male, ex-smoker with **progressive exertional dyspnea**, dry cough, **bibasal fine 'velcro' crackles**, and finger clubbing; restrictive spirometry with reduced DLCO.

en-pulmo.q: What HRCT pattern defines usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)?
en-pulmo.a: **Subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing**, with or without traction bronchiectasis. A typical UIP pattern in the right clinical context allows IPF diagnosis without biopsy.

en-pulmo.q: What is the pharmacologic treatment of IPF?
en-pulmo.a: **Antifibrotics: nintedanib or pirfenidone** slow FVC decline. **Avoid corticosteroids and immunosuppression** (harmful in IPF, PANTHER trial).

en-pulmo.q: What pulmonary function pattern is typical of ILD?
en-pulmo.a: **Restrictive**: reduced FVC and TLC with **normal or raised FEV1/FVC**, and **reduced DLCO** (gas transfer).

en-pulmo.q: What is hypersensitivity pneumonitis and give classic exposures?
en-pulmo.a: An immune-mediated ILD from **inhaled organic antigens**: bird proteins (bird fancier's lung), moldy hay (farmer's lung), hot tubs, and molds. Key treatment: **antigen avoidance**; steroids in selected cases.

en-pulmo.q: Which drugs commonly cause pulmonary fibrosis?
en-pulmo.a: **Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin**, busulfan, and cyclophosphamide; also checkpoint inhibitors (pneumonitis).

en-pulmo.q: What are the typical features of pulmonary sarcoidosis?
en-pulmo.a: Non-caseating granulomas; **bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy**, upper-zone perilymphatic nodules, erythema nodosum, uveitis, **hypercalcemia**, and raised ACE. Löfgren syndrome (BHL, erythema nodosum, arthritis, fever) has a good prognosis.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: which pneumoconiosis increases the risk of tuberculosis?
en-pulmo.a: **Silicosis** — upper-lobe nodules and **eggshell calcification** of hilar nodes; increases TB risk, so screen for latent TB. Asbestosis is lower-lobe with pleural plaques.

en-pulmo.q: Who is eligible for lung cancer screening under USPSTF 2021?
en-pulmo.a: Adults **aged 50–80** with **≥20 pack-years** who currently smoke or **quit within the past 15 years**; annual **low-dose CT**. ACS 2023 removed the years-since-quitting criterion.

en-pulmo.q: What is the main mortality benefit shown by lung cancer screening trials?
en-pulmo.a: Low-dose CT reduced lung cancer mortality by **~20% (NLST)** and ~24% in men (NELSON) compared with CXR or no screening.

en-pulmo.q: What features of a pulmonary nodule suggest malignancy?
en-pulmo.a: **Size (larger)**, **spiculated margins**, upper-lobe location, **growth on serial imaging**, part-solid morphology, older age, smoking history, and emphysema. Calcification patterns (central, popcorn) favor benign.

en-pulmo.q: What is the follow-up for an incidental solid nodule <6 mm in a low-risk adult (Fleischner)?
en-pulmo.a: **No routine follow-up** required; in high-risk patients, optional CT at 12 months.

en-pulmo.q: Which risk models help estimate malignancy probability in nodules?
en-pulmo.a: **Brock (PanCan) model** for initial assessment and **Herder model** after PET-CT (BTS). Both incorporate nodule and patient characteristics.

en-pulmo.q: Which lung cancer type is associated with SIADH and Cushing syndrome?
en-pulmo.a: **Small cell lung cancer** — central, smoking-related, rapid growth; also Lambert-Eaton syndrome. Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to **PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia**.

en-pulmo.q: What is the most common lung cancer in never-smokers?
en-pulmo.a: **Adenocarcinoma** — often peripheral; check for driver mutations (**EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS**, etc.) and PD-L1 to guide targeted therapy/immunotherapy.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: what does a solid nodule stable for 2 years on CT imply, and does this apply to ground-glass nodules?
en-pulmo.a: Solid nodules stable ≥2 years are generally benign. **Subsolid (ground-glass) nodules** can be slow-growing adenocarcinoma spectrum, so Fleischner recommends **follow-up up to 5 years**.

en-pulmo.q: What are Light's criteria for an exudate?
en-pulmo.a: Exudate if **any**: pleural/serum **protein >0.5**, pleural/serum **LDH >0.6**, or pleural LDH **>2/3 of the upper limit** of normal serum LDH.

en-pulmo.q: What are common causes of transudative pleural effusions?
en-pulmo.a: **Heart failure** (most common), **cirrhosis** (hepatic hydrothorax), nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia, and peritoneal dialysis.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: why may a diuresed heart failure effusion meet Light's criteria for exudate?
en-pulmo.a: Diuresis concentrates pleural protein. Use a **serum-pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL** (or protein gradient >3.1 g/dL) or NT-proBNP to confirm a transudate.

en-pulmo.q: Which pleural fluid findings indicate a complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage?
en-pulmo.a: **pH <7.2**, frank pus (empyema), or positive Gram stain/culture. Low glucose and high LDH also support complicated infection.

en-pulmo.q: What is the role of intrapleural therapy in pleural infection?
en-pulmo.a: **Tissue plasminogen activator plus DNase** (MIST-2) improves drainage in pleural infection failing chest-tube drainage; surgical (VATS) decortication if unsuccessful.

en-pulmo.q: What investigation is first-line to guide pleural aspiration?
en-pulmo.a: **Thoracic ultrasound** — improves yield and reduces pneumothorax and organ puncture (BTS recommends ultrasound guidance for all pleural procedures).

en-pulmo.q: Which pleural fluid finding suggests chylothorax?
en-pulmo.a: Milky fluid with **triglycerides >110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L)** and chylomicrons; causes include lymphoma and thoracic duct trauma.

en-pulmo.q: What is first-line management of a recurrent symptomatic malignant pleural effusion?
en-pulmo.a: **Indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis** (via chest drain or thoracoscopy), guided by lung re-expansion and patient preference; trapped lung favors an indwelling catheter.

en-pulmo.q: How is obstructive sleep apnea severity graded by AHI?
en-pulmo.a: Apnea-hypopnea index per hour: **mild 5–14**, **moderate 15–29**, **severe ≥30** events/h.

en-pulmo.q: What is the STOP-BANG questionnaire?
en-pulmo.a: Screening tool: **S**noring, **T**iredness, **O**bserved apneas, high blood **P**ressure, **B**MI >35, **A**ge >50, **N**eck >40 cm, male **G**ender; score ≥3 suggests increased OSA risk.

en-pulmo.q: What is first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe symptomatic OSA?
en-pulmo.a: **Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)** plus weight loss, alcohol avoidance, and sleep position measures. Mandibular advancement devices for mild–moderate OSA or CPAP intolerance.

en-pulmo.q: Which cardiovascular conditions are associated with untreated OSA?
en-pulmo.a: **Resistant hypertension**, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, stroke, and coronary disease. OSA is a common secondary cause of hypertension.

en-pulmo.q: What is the diagnostic test for OSA?
en-pulmo.a: **Polysomnography** (gold standard) or home sleep apnea testing (respiratory polygraphy) in uncomplicated patients with high pretest probability.

en-pulmo.q: What is the Epworth Sleepiness Scale used for?
en-pulmo.a: A questionnaire measuring **daytime sleepiness** (score 0–24; >10 indicates excessive sleepiness). It does not diagnose OSA.

en-pulmo.q: What defines obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
en-pulmo.a: **BMI ≥30** with **daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 ≥45 mmHg / 6 kPa)** not explained by other causes; most have coexisting OSA. Treat with PAP (CPAP or NIV) and weight loss.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: what must you advise an OSA patient with excessive sleepiness who drives?
en-pulmo.a: Excessive sleepiness impairs driving; patients should **not drive while sleepy** and must follow local licensing rules (e.g., DVLA notification in the UK for moderate–severe OSA with sleepiness).

en-pulmo.q: What is the standard regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB?
en-pulmo.a: **2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin (rifampin), pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE)**, followed by **4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin**. A 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen is an alternative (WHO/CDC).

en-pulmo.q: What are key adverse effects of first-line TB drugs?
en-pulmo.a: **Isoniazid**: peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine), hepatitis. **Rifampicin**: orange secretions, hepatitis, CYP induction. **Pyrazinamide**: hepatitis, hyperuricemia/gout. **Ethambutol**: optic neuritis (red-green color loss).

en-pulmo.q: How is latent TB infection diagnosed?
en-pulmo.a: **Interferon-gamma release assay** or **tuberculin skin test**, after excluding active TB (symptoms, chest X-ray). IGRA is preferred after BCG vaccination.

en-pulmo.q: What are treatment options for latent TB infection?
en-pulmo.a: **3 months of isoniazid plus rifapentine weekly (3HP)**, **3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin (3HR)**, **4 months of rifampicin (4R)**, or **6–9 months of isoniazid**.

en-pulmo.q: What is the preferred initial diagnostic test for pulmonary TB?
en-pulmo.a: **Sputum nucleic acid amplification test (e.g., Xpert MTB/RIF)** plus smear microscopy and **culture** (gold standard, allows full susceptibility testing). Xpert detects rifampicin resistance.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: why must you screen for latent TB before starting anti-TNF therapy?
en-pulmo.a: **TNF-α inhibitors** impair granuloma maintenance and carry a high risk of **TB reactivation**, often extrapulmonary or disseminated. Treat latent TB before or concurrently.

en-pulmo.q: What drug interaction is critical with rifampicin?
en-pulmo.a: Rifampicin is a **potent CYP3A4 inducer** — reduces levels of **oral contraceptives**, warfarin, DOACs, antiretrovirals (protease inhibitors), and corticosteroids; advise non-hormonal contraception.

en-pulmo.q: What is the typical chest X-ray finding in reactivation pulmonary TB?
en-pulmo.a: **Upper-lobe (apical/posterior segment) infiltrates with cavitation**. Primary TB shows a Ghon focus with hilar lymphadenopathy (Ghon complex); miliary TB shows diffuse micronodules.

en-pulmo.q: How are type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure defined?
en-pulmo.a: **Type 1 (hypoxemic)**: PaO2 <8 kPa (60 mmHg) with normal or low PaCO2. **Type 2 (hypercapnic)**: PaO2 <8 kPa with **PaCO2 >6.0 kPa (45 mmHg)** (some US sources use >50 mmHg).

en-pulmo.q: What is the alveolar-arterial (A–a) gradient and its significance?
en-pulmo.a: PAO2 − PaO2; PAO2 = FiO2 × (Patm − PH2O) − PaCO2/0.8. **A normal gradient** in hypoxemia suggests **hypoventilation or low FiO2**; a raised gradient suggests V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment.

en-pulmo.q: How do you calculate the anion gap and its normal range?
en-pulmo.a: **AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻)**, normal approximately 8–12 mmol/L (lab dependent); correct for low albumin (+2.5 per 1 g/dL decrease).

en-pulmo.q: What is Winter's formula?
en-pulmo.a: Expected PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis = **1.5 × HCO3⁻ + 8 (± 2) mmHg**. Higher PaCO2 indicates concomitant respiratory acidosis; lower indicates respiratory alkalosis.

en-pulmo.q: What are causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis?
en-pulmo.a: **Lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis (DKA, alcohol, starvation), renal failure, toxins** (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, acetaminophen-associated pyroglutamic acidosis). Mnemonic GOLDMARK.

en-pulmo.q: What defines ARDS according to the Berlin definition?
en-pulmo.a: Onset within **1 week** of insult, **bilateral opacities** not fully explained by effusions/collapse, respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure, and **PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mmHg with PEEP ≥5 cmH2O** (mild 201–300, moderate 101–200, severe ≤100).

en-pulmo.q: What ventilation strategy improves survival in ARDS?
en-pulmo.a: **Lung-protective ventilation**: tidal volume **6 mL/kg predicted body weight**, **plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O**, adequate PEEP, and **prone positioning** for 12–16 h/day in moderate–severe ARDS.

en-pulmo.q: Exam trap: why can pulse oximetry be falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide poisoning?
en-pulmo.a: Standard oximeters cannot distinguish **carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin**, giving normal SpO2 despite hypoxia. Use **CO-oximetry** on blood gas; treat with 100% oxygen.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the KDIGO criteria for acute kidney injury?
en-nefro-endo.a: Any of: serum creatinine rise **≥0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) within 48 h**, rise to **≥1.5× baseline** within the prior 7 days, or urine output **<0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h**.

en-nefro-endo.q: Which findings define KDIGO stage 3 AKI?
en-nefro-endo.a: Creatinine **≥3× baseline**, or creatinine ≥4.0 mg/dL (354 µmol/L), or initiation of kidney replacement therapy, or urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 h, or anuria ≥12 h.

en-nefro-endo.q: Exam trap: why can FENa mislead in a patient with AKI on furosemide, and what is the alternative?
en-nefro-endo.a: Loop diuretics increase urinary sodium, falsely raising FENa even in prerenal states. Use **fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea)**: <35% suggests prerenal AKI.

en-nefro-endo.q: Match urinary casts to their classic cause: muddy brown granular, RBC casts, WBC casts.
en-nefro-endo.a: **Muddy brown granular casts** = acute tubular necrosis; **RBC casts** = glomerulonephritis; **WBC casts** = acute interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis.

en-nefro-endo.q: What single bedside test should be done early in every unexplained AKI to exclude a reversible cause?
en-nefro-endo.a: Assess for obstruction: **bladder scan/catheter and renal ultrasound** to look for urinary retention or hydronephrosis (postrenal AKI).

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the classic indications for urgent dialysis in AKI (AEIOU)?
en-nefro-endo.a: Refractory **A**cidosis, **E**lectrolytes (refractory hyperkalemia), **I**ntoxications (e.g., lithium, toxic alcohols, salicylates), refractory fluid **O**verload, and **U**remic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding).

en-nefro-endo.q: A patient on a PPI develops AKI with fever, rash, and eosinophilia. Diagnosis and management?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis** (common culprits: PPIs, beta-lactams, NSAIDs). Stop the offending drug; corticosteroids are often used if no prompt recovery, though evidence is limited.

en-nefro-endo.q: Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows no RBCs after a crush injury. What is happening?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Rhabdomyolysis** with myoglobinuria (dipstick detects heme). Confirm with a markedly elevated CK and treat with early, aggressive isotonic fluids while monitoring potassium.

en-nefro-endo.q: How is chronic kidney disease defined by KDIGO?
en-nefro-endo.a: Abnormal kidney structure or function present **>3 months** with health implications, e.g., **eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²** or albuminuria **ACR ≥30 mg/g (≥3 mg/mmol)**.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the KDIGO albuminuria categories A1–A3?
en-nefro-endo.a: **A1** ACR <30 mg/g (<3 mg/mmol), **A2** 30–300 mg/g (3–30 mg/mmol), **A3** >300 mg/g (>30 mg/mmol). CKD is staged by both GFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3).

en-nefro-endo.q: After starting an ACE inhibitor in albuminuric CKD, creatinine rises 20%. What should you do?
en-nefro-endo.a: Continue it. A creatinine rise **up to 30%** after starting RAS blockade is expected (hemodynamic) and acceptable; recheck labs and investigate only larger rises or hyperkalemia.

en-nefro-endo.q: Which CKD patients should receive an SGLT2 inhibitor per KDIGO 2024?
en-nefro-endo.a: Type 2 diabetes with CKD and **eGFR ≥20**, and CKD without diabetes with eGFR ≥20 plus ACR ≥200 mg/g or heart failure. Benefits are largely independent of glucose lowering.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is finerenone and when is it indicated?
en-nefro-endo.a: A **nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist** that reduces kidney and cardiovascular events in **type 2 diabetes with albuminuric CKD** on maximal RAS blockade, when potassium is normal.

en-nefro-endo.q: Describe the classic mineral pattern of CKD–mineral and bone disorder.
en-nefro-endo.a: **High phosphate, high FGF23, low calcitriol**, low-normal calcium, and **secondary hyperparathyroidism**, leading to renal osteodystrophy and vascular calcification.

en-nefro-endo.q: What must be checked and corrected before starting an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in CKD anemia?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Iron status** (ferritin, transferrin saturation) and other causes of anemia; replete iron first. KDIGO advises against targeting hemoglobin above ~11.5 g/dL because of stroke and thrombosis risk.

en-nefro-endo.q: How should metformin be adjusted in CKD?
en-nefro-endo.a: Contraindicated at **eGFR <30**; do not start at eGFR 30–45, and review/reduce dose if eGFR falls to 30–45. Hold during acute illness or iodinated contrast with unstable kidney function.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the first step in evaluating hyponatremia?
en-nefro-endo.a: Measure **serum osmolality** to confirm hypotonic hyponatremia and exclude pseudohyponatremia (severe hyperlipidemia, paraproteinemia) and hypertonic causes (hyperglycemia, mannitol).

en-nefro-endo.q: How does hyperglycemia affect measured serum sodium?
en-nefro-endo.a: Glucose draws water out of cells, diluting sodium. Sodium falls about **1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL** glucose above 100 (some use 2.4 at very high glucose).

en-nefro-endo.q: A hyponatremic patient has urine osmolality <100 mOsm/kg. What are the likely causes?
en-nefro-endo.a: Maximal dilution, so ADH is suppressed: **primary polydipsia** or **low solute intake** (beer potomania, "tea and toast" diet).

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the essential diagnostic features of SIADH?
en-nefro-endo.a: Hypotonic hyponatremia, **inappropriately concentrated urine (osm >100)**, **urine Na >30 mEq/L**, clinical euvolemia, and exclusion of hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and recent diuretic use.

en-nefro-endo.q: How do you treat hyponatremia with seizures or coma?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Hypertonic (3%) saline 100–150 mL IV bolus** over 10–20 min, repeated up to 2–3 times as needed, aiming for a rapid rise of **4–6 mEq/L**, which usually stops symptoms.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the maximum safe sodium correction rate, and which patients are highest risk?
en-nefro-endo.a: Generally **≤8 mEq/L in 24 h** in high-risk patients (guidelines vary, some allow 10–12 in low-risk). High risk: Na ≤105, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease. Overcorrection causes **osmotic demyelination**.

en-nefro-endo.q: Exam trap: why can 0.9% saline worsen hyponatremia in SIADH?
en-nefro-endo.a: When urine osmolality exceeds that of the infused fluid, the kidney excretes the salt but retains the water (**desalination**), lowering sodium further.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is first-line treatment of chronic mild SIADH, and what are second-line options?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Fluid restriction** (often <800–1000 mL/day) and treating the cause. Second-line: **oral urea** or a vaptan (tolvaptan; avoid in liver disease and monitor for overcorrection).

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the first test in a patient with a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L?
en-nefro-endo.a: An immediate **12-lead ECG**, plus a repeat sample if hemolysis or pseudohyperkalemia is suspected. ECG changes mandate emergency treatment regardless of the exact level.

en-nefro-endo.q: Describe the classic ECG progression of worsening hyperkalemia.
en-nefro-endo.a: **Peaked T waves** → PR prolongation and P-wave flattening → **QRS widening** → sine-wave pattern → ventricular fibrillation or asystole. ECG findings correlate poorly with the exact potassium level.

en-nefro-endo.q: What does IV calcium do in hyperkalemia, and does it lower potassium?
en-nefro-endo.a: It **stabilizes the cardiac membrane** within minutes but does **not** lower potassium. Give 10% calcium gluconate IV (UK guidance 30 mL), repeat if ECG changes persist.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the standard insulin–glucose regimen to shift potassium intracellularly?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Regular insulin 10 units IV with 25 g glucose** (e.g., 50 mL of 50% dextrose). Onset 15–30 min; monitor glucose closely for hypoglycemia, especially in CKD.

en-nefro-endo.q: Which treatments actually remove potassium from the body?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Potassium binders** (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer), loop diuretics if kidney function allows, and **hemodialysis**, the definitive option in refractory or kidney-failure cases.

en-nefro-endo.q: List common drug causes of hyperkalemia.
en-nefro-endo.a: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, MRAs (spironolactone), potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride), **trimethoprim**, **heparin**, NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors, and beta-blockers.

en-nefro-endo.q: Exam trap: why must potassium be rechecked 1–2 hours and again several hours after insulin–glucose therapy?
en-nefro-endo.a: Insulin and beta-agonists only **shift** potassium into cells; effects wane after about 4–6 h, causing **rebound hyperkalemia** unless potassium is also removed.

en-nefro-endo.q: When is sodium bicarbonate useful for hyperkalemia?
en-nefro-endo.a: Only as an adjunct when there is **concurrent metabolic acidosis**. It is not a reliable first-line agent for shifting potassium on its own.

en-nefro-endo.q: How is the anion gap calculated and corrected for albumin?
en-nefro-endo.a: **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃)**, normal about 8–12 (lab-dependent). Add about **2.5 for every 1 g/dL** that albumin is below 4 g/dL, or a high gap can be missed.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is Winter's formula and why use it?
en-nefro-endo.a: Expected **PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2** in metabolic acidosis. A higher PaCO₂ means concurrent respiratory acidosis; a lower one means concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis (GOLDMARK)?
en-nefro-endo.a: **G**lycols, **O**xoproline (chronic acetaminophen), **L**-lactate, **D**-lactate, **M**ethanol, **A**spirin, **R**enal failure, **K**etoacidosis.

en-nefro-endo.q: A patient with high anion gap acidosis has an osmolar gap of 25. What should you suspect?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Toxic alcohol ingestion** (methanol or ethylene glycol). Give **fomepizole** and consider hemodialysis; ethylene glycol classically causes calcium oxalate crystals and AKI.

en-nefro-endo.q: How does the urine anion gap distinguish diarrhea from renal tubular acidosis in normal anion gap acidosis?
en-nefro-endo.a: UAG = urine Na + K − Cl. **Negative** UAG means high ammonium excretion (**diarrhea**); **positive** UAG means impaired acid excretion (**distal RTA**).

en-nefro-endo.q: Compare the three main RTA types.
en-nefro-endo.a: **Type 1 (distal)**: urine pH >5.5, hypokalemia, stones. **Type 2 (proximal)**: bicarbonate wasting, often Fanconi syndrome. **Type 4**: hypoaldosteronism with **hyperkalemia**, common in diabetic CKD.

en-nefro-endo.q: How does urine chloride classify metabolic alkalosis?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Urine Cl <20 mEq/L**: chloride-responsive (vomiting, NG suction, prior diuretics) → saline. **Urine Cl >20**: chloride-resistant (mineralocorticoid excess, current diuretics, Bartter/Gitelman).

en-nefro-endo.q: What acid–base pattern is classic for salicylate poisoning in adults?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Mixed respiratory alkalosis** (direct respiratory center stimulation) **plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis**. Treat with urinary alkalinization; dialyze for severe toxicity.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the ADA diagnostic criteria for diabetes?
en-nefro-endo.a: **A1c ≥6.5%**, fasting glucose **≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L)**, 2-h OGTT glucose **≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L)**, or random glucose ≥200 with classic symptoms. Confirm abnormal tests unless unequivocal.

en-nefro-endo.q: Exam trap: when is HbA1c unreliable for diagnosis or monitoring?
en-nefro-endo.a: Altered red cell turnover: **hemoglobinopathies, iron deficiency, hemolysis, recent transfusion or bleeding, pregnancy, advanced CKD/ESA use**. Use glucose-based tests instead.

en-nefro-endo.q: In type 2 diabetes with heart failure or CKD, which drug class is preferred regardless of A1c?
en-nefro-endo.a: An **SGLT2 inhibitor** with proven benefit (ADA/KDIGO). In established ASCVD, an SGLT2 inhibitor or **GLP-1 receptor agonist** with proven cardiovascular benefit is recommended independent of metformin use.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the general A1c target for nonpregnant adults with diabetes?
en-nefro-endo.a: **<7%** for most. Individualize: less stringent (e.g., **<8%**) for older adults, limited life expectancy, or frequent hypoglycemia; tighter if achievable safely.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the key long-term adverse effects of metformin?
en-nefro-endo.a: GI upset (common, reduced with extended-release), **vitamin B12 deficiency** with long-term use, and rare **lactic acidosis** mainly with severe kidney impairment or hypoperfusion.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the main contraindication to GLP-1 receptor agonists?
en-nefro-endo.a: Personal or family history of **medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2**. Use caution with prior pancreatitis and severe gastroparesis; they can delay gastric emptying before anesthesia.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the key adverse effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, and when should they be held?
en-nefro-endo.a: Genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, and **euglycemic DKA**. Hold during acute illness and **3–4 days before scheduled surgery** (4 days for ertugliflozin).

en-nefro-endo.q: What annual complication screening is recommended in type 2 diabetes?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Urine ACR and eGFR**, **dilated retinal exam** (every 1–2 years if normal), and a **comprehensive foot exam** including monofilament testing, plus lipid and blood pressure review.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the 2024 consensus diagnostic criteria for DKA?
en-nefro-endo.a: Glucose **≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L)** or known diabetes, **β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L** (or urine ketones ≥2+), and **pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mEq/L**.

en-nefro-endo.q: What defines hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)?
en-nefro-endo.a: Glucose **≥600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L)**, effective osmolality **>300 mOsm/kg** (or total >320), no significant ketonemia, **pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15**. Often older patients with marked dehydration and altered mentation.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the first treatment step in DKA?
en-nefro-endo.a: **IV isotonic crystalloid**, typically 1–1.5 L in the first hour, then adjusted to volume status and sodium. Check potassium before starting insulin.

en-nefro-endo.q: How does potassium guide insulin therapy in DKA?
en-nefro-endo.a: If **K <3.5 mEq/L, hold insulin** and replace potassium first (risk of fatal hypokalemia). Add potassium to fluids when K is between 3.5 and about 5.0–5.3.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the standard IV insulin regimen in DKA and when is dextrose added?
en-nefro-endo.a: Fixed-rate regular insulin **0.1 units/kg/h IV**. Add dextrose when glucose falls below about **250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L)** and continue insulin until ketoacidosis resolves.

en-nefro-endo.q: When is DKA resolved and how do you transition off IV insulin?
en-nefro-endo.a: Resolution: **pH ≥7.3, bicarbonate ≥18, β-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L** (2024 consensus). Give subcutaneous basal insulin **1–2 h before stopping** the infusion to prevent rebound.

en-nefro-endo.q: When is sodium bicarbonate indicated in DKA?
en-nefro-endo.a: Only for severe acidemia, **pH <7.0** (2024 consensus). Routine bicarbonate does not improve outcomes and may worsen hypokalemia.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are common precipitants of DKA and HHS?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Infection** and **insulin omission** are most common; also new-onset diabetes, MI, stroke, pancreatitis, and drugs (SGLT2 inhibitors, corticosteroids, antipsychotics).

en-nefro-endo.q: What lab pattern defines primary hypothyroidism, and what is the commonest cause in iodine-sufficient regions?
en-nefro-endo.a: **High TSH with low free T4**. Most commonly **Hashimoto thyroiditis**, usually with positive anti-TPO antibodies.

en-nefro-endo.q: How should levothyroxine be started and monitored?
en-nefro-endo.a: Healthy younger adults: about **1.6 mcg/kg/day** on an empty stomach. Older adults or coronary disease: start low (**25–50 mcg/day**). Recheck TSH after **6–8 weeks**.

en-nefro-endo.q: How should levothyroxine be adjusted when a hypothyroid woman becomes pregnant?
en-nefro-endo.a: Increase the dose promptly by about **25–30%** (e.g., two extra doses per week) once pregnancy is confirmed, and monitor TSH every 4 weeks in the first half of pregnancy.

en-nefro-endo.q: What findings confirm Graves disease?
en-nefro-endo.a: Suppressed TSH, high free T4/T3, **positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb)**, and diffusely increased radioiodine uptake. Orbitopathy and pretibial myxedema are specific to Graves.

en-nefro-endo.q: Painful tender goiter, high ESR, and hyperthyroidism after a viral illness. Diagnosis and treatment?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis** with **low radioiodine uptake**. Treat with NSAIDs or steroids and beta-blockers; antithyroid drugs are ineffective because hormone is released, not synthesized.

en-nefro-endo.q: Which antithyroid drug is first-line, and when is propylthiouracil preferred?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Methimazole** is first-line. **PTU** is preferred in the **first trimester** and in thyroid storm. Both can cause **agranulocytosis**: stop and check a CBC if fever or sore throat.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the correct order of drugs in thyroid storm?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Beta-blocker** (propranolol), then a **thionamide** (PTU preferred), then **iodine at least 1 hour after** the thionamide, plus **hydrocortisone** and supportive care; treat the precipitant.

en-nefro-endo.q: In myxedema coma, what must be given with IV levothyroxine?
en-nefro-endo.a: **IV hydrocortisone** until coexisting adrenal insufficiency is excluded, because thyroid hormone can precipitate adrenal crisis. Also supportive care for hypothermia, hypoventilation, and hyponatremia.

en-nefro-endo.q: What features distinguish primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)?
en-nefro-endo.a: Low cortisol with **high ACTH**, **hyperpigmentation**, and mineralocorticoid deficiency: **hyponatremia, hyperkalemia**, hypotension, salt craving. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest cause in high-income countries.

en-nefro-endo.q: How is adrenal insufficiency confirmed?
en-nefro-endo.a: **ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test**, 250 mcg IV/IM: peak cortisol below about **18 mcg/dL (500 nmol/L)** suggests insufficiency; newer specific assays use lower cutoffs (~14–15 mcg/dL).

en-nefro-endo.q: How do you treat suspected adrenal crisis?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately**, then 200 mg/24 h (e.g., 50 mg every 6 h), plus IV isotonic saline. Never delay treatment for diagnostic tests.

en-nefro-endo.q: Why does secondary adrenal insufficiency lack hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation?
en-nefro-endo.a: ACTH is low, so no pigmentation, and **aldosterone is regulated by renin–angiotensin**, which is intact. The commonest cause is **withdrawal of exogenous glucocorticoids**.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the first-line screening tests for Cushing syndrome?
en-nefro-endo.a: Any of: **1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression** (cortisol >1.8 mcg/dL / 50 nmol/L abnormal), **late-night salivary cortisol**, or **24-h urinary free cortisol**. Exclude exogenous steroids first.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome?
en-nefro-endo.a: **ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease)**. The most common cause overall is exogenous glucocorticoid use.

en-nefro-endo.q: How is primary aldosteronism screened and confirmed?
en-nefro-endo.a: Screen with the **aldosterone-to-renin ratio**, confirm with a suppression test (e.g., saline infusion) if needed, then CT and **adrenal vein sampling** before surgery. Endocrine Society 2025 suggests screening all hypertensive patients.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the key preoperative rule for pheochromocytoma?
en-nefro-endo.a: Diagnose with **plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines**. Start **alpha-blockade first** (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 7–14 days; beta-blockers only after, to avoid unopposed alpha crisis.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are the most common causes of hypercalcemia in outpatients versus inpatients?
en-nefro-endo.a: Outpatients: **primary hyperparathyroidism**. Hospitalized patients: **malignancy**. Together they cause about 90% of cases; check **PTH** first.

en-nefro-endo.q: How is total calcium corrected for low albumin?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL)**. The correction is imperfect; measure **ionized calcium** when accuracy matters.

en-nefro-endo.q: What is the initial treatment of severe symptomatic hypercalcemia?
en-nefro-endo.a: **IV isotonic saline**, **calcitonin** for rapid effect (tachyphylaxis within ~48 h), and an **IV bisphosphonate** (zoledronic acid 4 mg IV). Denosumab if kidney failure; loop diuretics only after volume repletion.

en-nefro-endo.q: What are surgical indications in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism?
en-nefro-endo.a: Calcium **>1 mg/dL above upper limit**, osteoporosis or vertebral fracture, **eGFR <60**, kidney stones/nephrocalcinosis or hypercalciuria, or **age <50**. All symptomatic patients qualify.

en-nefro-endo.q: Mild hypercalcemia, normal PTH, and very low urinary calcium. What must be excluded before surgery?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia** (inactivating CaSR mutation): calcium/creatinine clearance ratio usually **<0.01**. It is benign and parathyroidectomy does not help.

en-nefro-endo.q: Hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH in a patient with lung squamous cell carcinoma. Mechanism?
en-nefro-endo.a: **PTH-related peptide (PTHrP)** secretion (humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy). Other malignant mechanisms: osteolytic metastases, myeloma, and lymphoma producing calcitriol.

en-nefro-endo.q: Exam trap: hypocalcemia fails to correct despite IV calcium. What should you check?
en-nefro-endo.a: **Magnesium**. Hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and action, so calcium stays low until magnesium is replaced.

en-nefro-endo.q: Differentiate secondary from tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
en-nefro-endo.a: **Secondary**: appropriate high PTH from low calcium or vitamin D, or CKD. **Tertiary**: autonomous PTH secretion with **hypercalcemia** after long-standing secondary disease, classically after kidney transplant.

en-gastro.q: Which upper GI bleeding patients can be managed as outpatients?
en-gastro.a: Those with a **Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0–1** (ACG; NICE considers early discharge at score 0), who are at very low risk of needing intervention or dying.

en-gastro.q: What hemoglobin threshold should trigger transfusion in acute GI bleeding?
en-gastro.a: Restrictive: **Hb <7 g/dL** for most patients; a higher threshold (around **8 g/dL**) with cardiovascular disease. Liberal transfusion increases rebleeding in variceal bleeding.

en-gastro.q: Which endoscopic ulcer findings are high-risk and warrant endoscopic therapy?
en-gastro.a: **Active spurting or oozing** (Forrest Ia/Ib) and a **non-bleeding visible vessel** (IIa); an adherent clot (IIb) may be treated. Flat spots and clean bases are low risk.

en-gastro.q: What PPI regimen follows successful endoscopic hemostasis of a high-risk ulcer?
en-gastro.a: **High-dose PPI for 72 hours**, e.g., 80 mg IV bolus then continuous infusion or intermittent high-dose dosing, followed by twice-daily oral PPI.

en-gastro.q: List the key steps in managing suspected acute variceal bleeding.
en-gastro.a: Resuscitate, **vasoactive drug** (octreotide or terlipressin), **antibiotic prophylaxis** (e.g., ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily), and **band ligation within 12 h**. Consider pre-emptive TIPS in high-risk patients.

en-gastro.q: Which drug given before endoscopy improves mucosal visualization in upper GI bleeding?
en-gastro.a: **IV erythromycin** (a motilin agonist), typically 250 mg IV 30–120 minutes before endoscopy, to clear blood from the stomach.

en-gastro.q: Exam trap: brisk hematochezia with hypotension. Why consider an upper GI source?
en-gastro.a: About 10–15% of severe hematochezia comes from a **brisk upper GI bleed**. A high BUN-to-creatinine ratio supports it; perform upper endoscopy if suspicion exists.

en-gastro.q: What is the most common cause of acute lower GI bleeding in adults and how is it evaluated?
en-gastro.a: **Diverticular bleeding** (painless). Colonoscopy after bowel prep in stable patients; **CT angiography** first if hemodynamically unstable or bleeding actively.

en-gastro.q: What are the five components of the Child-Pugh score?
en-gastro.a: **Bilirubin, albumin, INR (or PT), ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy**. MELD instead uses bilirubin, INR, creatinine, and sodium (MELD 3.0 adds albumin and sex).

en-gastro.q: How do you interpret the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG)?
en-gastro.a: **SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL** = portal hypertension. Then ascitic protein **<2.5 g/dL** suggests cirrhosis; **≥2.5 g/dL** suggests cardiac ascites or Budd-Chiari. SAAG <1.1 suggests peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB, or pancreatitis.

en-gastro.q: What defines spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and how is it treated?
en-gastro.a: Ascitic **neutrophils ≥250 cells/mm³**. Treat with a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime) plus **IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3** to reduce kidney failure.

en-gastro.q: How much albumin should follow large-volume paracentesis?
en-gastro.a: For paracentesis **>5 L**, give **6–8 g of albumin per liter removed** to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.

en-gastro.q: What is first-line diuretic therapy for cirrhotic ascites?
en-gastro.a: **Sodium restriction (about 2 g/day)** plus **spironolactone and furosemide in a 100:40 ratio**, titrated to weight loss; fluid restriction only if sodium is <125 mEq/L.

en-gastro.q: How is hepatic encephalopathy treated and prevented?
en-gastro.a: Identify precipitants (infection, bleeding, constipation, sedatives, hypokalemia). **Lactulose** titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily; add **rifaximin 550 mg twice daily** to prevent recurrence.

en-gastro.q: How is hepatorenal syndrome–AKI treated?
en-gastro.a: After stopping diuretics and giving albumin (1 g/kg) without response, treat with **terlipressin (or norepinephrine) plus albumin**. Liver transplant is the definitive therapy.

en-gastro.q: What hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance is recommended in cirrhosis?
en-gastro.a: **Ultrasound every 6 months**, with or without AFP (AASLD recommends adding AFP; EASL leaves it optional).

en-gastro.q: What criteria establish a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
en-gastro.a: Two of three: characteristic **epigastric pain** (often radiating to the back), **lipase or amylase >3× upper limit**, and characteristic imaging findings.

en-gastro.q: What are the leading causes of acute pancreatitis?
en-gastro.a: **Gallstones and alcohol** most often. Others: **triglycerides >1000 mg/dL**, post-ERCP, hypercalcemia, drugs (azathioprine, valproate), trauma, and autoimmune disease.

en-gastro.q: What fluid strategy is recommended in acute pancreatitis?
en-gastro.a: **Moderate, goal-directed lactated Ringer's**. The WATERFALL trial showed aggressive fluids caused more fluid overload without benefit; reassess volume status frequently.

en-gastro.q: Exam trap: should all patients with acute pancreatitis get a CT on admission?
en-gastro.a: No. CT is for **diagnostic uncertainty** or failure to improve after **48–72 h** (to assess necrosis). Get a **right upper quadrant ultrasound** at admission to look for gallstones.

en-gastro.q: How does the revised Atlanta classification grade severity?
en-gastro.a: **Mild**: no organ failure or complications. **Moderately severe**: transient organ failure (<48 h) or local complications. **Severe**: **persistent organ failure >48 h**.

en-gastro.q: When should feeding start in acute pancreatitis?
en-gastro.a: **Early oral feeding within 24 h** as tolerated in mild disease. If oral intake fails, **enteral** nutrition is preferred over parenteral.

en-gastro.q: Are prophylactic antibiotics recommended in necrotizing pancreatitis?
en-gastro.a: No. Give antibiotics only for suspected **infected necrosis** (e.g., gas in collections). Intervention is delayed about **4 weeks** until walled off, using a step-up, minimally invasive approach.

en-gastro.q: When should cholecystectomy and ERCP be done in gallstone pancreatitis?
en-gastro.a: **Cholecystectomy during the same admission** for mild disease. **Urgent ERCP** only with concurrent **cholangitis** (or persistent biliary obstruction).

en-gastro.q: Contrast the distribution and histology of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
en-gastro.a: **UC**: continuous mucosal inflammation starting in the **rectum**. **Crohn disease**: **transmural**, skip lesions anywhere mouth to anus (often terminal ileum), fistulas, strictures, noncaseating granulomas.

en-gastro.q: How does smoking affect ulcerative colitis versus Crohn disease?
en-gastro.a: Smoking is associated with **lower risk of UC** but **worsens Crohn disease**. Smoking cessation is strongly advised in Crohn disease.

en-gastro.q: How is acute severe ulcerative colitis defined (Truelove and Witts)?
en-gastro.a: **≥6 bloody stools/day** plus systemic toxicity: heart rate >90, temperature >37.8 °C, Hb <10.5 g/dL, or ESR >30 mm/h. Admit for IV steroids.

en-gastro.q: How is acute severe UC managed in hospital?
en-gastro.a: **IV corticosteroids** (e.g., methylprednisolone 60 mg/day), VTE prophylaxis, stool tests for C. difficile. Reassess around **day 3**: nonresponders need **infliximab or ciclosporin** rescue or colectomy.

en-gastro.q: What is first-line therapy for mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis?
en-gastro.a: **Mesalamine (5-ASA)**, oral plus rectal for best effect. Exam trap: 5-ASA has little role in Crohn disease.

en-gastro.q: What screening is required before starting anti-TNF or other immunosuppressive therapy?
en-gastro.a: **Latent tuberculosis** (IGRA), **hepatitis B** (HBsAg, anti-HBc), HIV and vaccination review. Check **TPMT/NUDT15** activity before thiopurines.

en-gastro.q: Which extraintestinal manifestation of IBD is closely linked to ulcerative colitis and colon cancer?
en-gastro.a: **Primary sclerosing cholangitis**. Others: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, episcleritis/uveitis, peripheral arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis.

en-gastro.q: When does colorectal cancer surveillance start in colitis?
en-gastro.a: Colonoscopy about **8 years after symptom onset** for colitis beyond the rectum, then every 1–5 years by risk. With **PSC, start at diagnosis and repeat annually**.

en-gastro.q: What are the two main causes of peptic ulcer disease?
en-gastro.a: **Helicobacter pylori** infection and **NSAIDs/aspirin**. Consider Zollinger-Ellison syndrome when ulcers are multiple, distal, or refractory.

en-gastro.q: Which noninvasive tests diagnose active H. pylori infection, and what interferes with them?
en-gastro.a: **Urea breath test** or **stool antigen**. Stop PPIs **2 weeks** and antibiotics/bismuth **4 weeks** before testing to avoid false negatives. Serology cannot confirm active infection.

en-gastro.q: What is the preferred first-line H. pylori regimen when antibiotic susceptibility is unknown?
en-gastro.a: **Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days**: PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole (ACG 2024). Clarithromycin triple therapy only if susceptibility is confirmed; rifabutin or vonoprazan–amoxicillin regimens are alternatives.

en-gastro.q: Should eradication of H. pylori be confirmed after treatment?
en-gastro.a: Yes. **Test of cure for everyone** with urea breath test or stool antigen **≥4 weeks after therapy** and after PPI withdrawal for 2 weeks.

en-gastro.q: Why is follow-up endoscopy often needed for gastric but not duodenal ulcers?
en-gastro.a: **Gastric ulcers can be malignant**; biopsy the ulcer and repeat endoscopy to confirm healing if suspicious or not biopsied adequately. Duodenal ulcers are rarely malignant.

en-gastro.q: Sudden severe epigastric pain with rigid abdomen in a patient on NSAIDs. First imaging and diagnosis?
en-gastro.a: **Perforated peptic ulcer**. Upright chest X-ray may show **free air under the diaphragm**; CT is more sensitive. Surgical emergency.

en-gastro.q: What suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and how is it screened?
en-gastro.a: Multiple or refractory ulcers, jejunal ulcers, **diarrhea**, and enlarged gastric folds. Screen with **fasting serum gastrin** (off PPI if safe); associated with **MEN1**.

en-gastro.q: How is ulcer risk reduced in high-risk patients who need NSAIDs?
en-gastro.a: Use the lowest dose, add a **PPI**, test and treat H. pylori. For highest risk (prior complicated ulcer), a **COX-2 inhibitor plus PPI**, or avoid NSAIDs.

en-gastro.q: How should typical GERD without alarm features be managed initially?
en-gastro.a: **Empiric PPI once daily for 8 weeks**, taken 30–60 minutes before breakfast, plus weight loss and head-of-bed elevation for nocturnal symptoms.

en-gastro.q: Which alarm features prompt endoscopy in suspected GERD?
en-gastro.a: **Dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding or iron deficiency anemia, persistent vomiting**, and new symptoms at older age (thresholds vary by guideline).

en-gastro.q: How is Barrett esophagus defined in the US?
en-gastro.a: Salmon-colored mucosa extending **≥1 cm above the gastroesophageal junction** with **intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells)** on biopsy (ACG). British guidelines do not require goblet cells.

en-gastro.q: Who should be screened for Barrett esophagus?
en-gastro.a: Chronic GERD plus **≥3 risk factors**: male sex, age >50, white race, smoking, central obesity, or family history of Barrett or esophageal adenocarcinoma (ACG).

en-gastro.q: How is nondysplastic Barrett esophagus managed?
en-gastro.a: PPI therapy and **surveillance endoscopy every 3–5 years**. Confirmed low- or high-grade dysplasia is treated with **endoscopic eradication therapy** (e.g., radiofrequency ablation).

en-gastro.q: What objective evidence confirms GERD in PPI-refractory symptoms?
en-gastro.a: **LA grade C or D esophagitis**, long-segment Barrett, peptic stricture, or **acid exposure time >6%** on ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI (Lyon consensus; Lyon 2.0 also accepts LA grade B).

en-gastro.q: What must be done before antireflux surgery?
en-gastro.a: Confirm GERD objectively (endoscopy and/or pH monitoring) and perform **esophageal manometry** to exclude **achalasia** or major motility disorders.

en-gastro.q: Which adverse associations with long-term PPIs are commonly cited, and how strong is the evidence?
en-gastro.a: C. difficile, **hypomagnesemia**, B12 deficiency, fractures, pneumonia. Most are **observational**; use the lowest effective dose and deprescribe when no indication, but do not withhold PPIs when indicated.

en-gastro.q: Interpret HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs positive.
en-gastro.a: **Immunity from vaccination**. Natural immunity from past infection shows **anti-HBc positive plus anti-HBs positive**.

en-gastro.q: Which serologic marker identifies acute hepatitis B, including the window period?
en-gastro.a: **IgM anti-HBc**. It is positive in acute infection and during the window period when HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared.

en-gastro.q: How is chronic hepatitis B defined?
en-gastro.a: **HBsAg persisting >6 months**. Management depends on HBV DNA, ALT, HBeAg status, and fibrosis stage.

en-gastro.q: What are first-line antiviral drugs for chronic hepatitis B?
en-gastro.a: **Entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, or tenofovir alafenamide**, all with a high barrier to resistance. Therapy usually suppresses but rarely eradicates HBV.

en-gastro.q: Exam trap: which HBV serology must be checked before rituximab or chemotherapy, and why?
en-gastro.a: **HBsAg and anti-HBc** (± anti-HBs). Rituximab and similar agents can cause **HBV reactivation**, even in HBsAg-negative/anti-HBc-positive patients; give antiviral prophylaxis or monitor per risk.

en-gastro.q: Who should be screened for hepatitis C, and how is infection confirmed?
en-gastro.a: **All adults at least once** (CDC ≥18; USPSTF 18–79) and **each pregnancy**. Screen with anti-HCV; confirm active infection with **HCV RNA**.

en-gastro.q: What are standard pangenotypic regimens for chronic hepatitis C?
en-gastro.a: **Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks** or **glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks** in most patients. **SVR12** (undetectable RNA 12 weeks after therapy) indicates cure.
