en-gastro.q: After HCV cure in a patient with cirrhosis, is HCC surveillance still needed?
en-gastro.a: Yes. **Continue ultrasound every 6 months**; HCC risk falls but persists after SVR in cirrhosis. Also check HBV status before DAAs because of reactivation risk.

en-gastro.q: What is the first-line screening test for celiac disease?
en-gastro.a: **IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA)** with a **total IgA level**, while the patient is eating gluten.

en-gastro.q: Exam trap: a patient has negative tTG-IgA but IgA deficiency. What next?
en-gastro.a: Use **IgG-based tests** (deamidated gliadin peptide IgG or tTG-IgG). IgA deficiency is more common in celiac disease.

en-gastro.q: How is celiac disease confirmed in adults?
en-gastro.a: **Duodenal biopsies** (multiple, including the bulb) showing **villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis** (Marsh). A no-biopsy pathway is accepted in children and in some adult guidelines.

en-gastro.q: What is the value of HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing?
en-gastro.a: A **high negative predictive value**: absence of both essentially excludes celiac disease. A positive result is common in the general population and does not confirm it.

en-gastro.q: What skin condition is pathognomonic for celiac disease, and how is it treated?
en-gastro.a: **Dermatitis herpetiformis**: intensely itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces with granular IgA in dermal papillae. Treat with a **gluten-free diet ± dapsone**.

en-gastro.q: Which conditions warrant celiac testing?
en-gastro.a: Unexplained **iron deficiency anemia**, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, osteoporosis, elevated transaminases, **type 1 diabetes**, autoimmune thyroid disease, Down or Turner syndrome, and first-degree relatives.

en-gastro.q: A treated patient has persistent symptoms. What is the most common cause?
en-gastro.a: **Ongoing gluten exposure**, often inadvertent. Then consider other causes and, rarely, **refractory celiac disease**; type 2 carries a risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.

en-gastro.q: Exam trap: why can testing be falsely negative in a patient already on a gluten-free diet?
en-gastro.a: Antibodies and mucosal changes normalize without gluten. A supervised **gluten challenge** over several weeks is needed before serology or biopsy.

en-gastro.q: At what age should average-risk adults begin colorectal cancer screening?
en-gastro.a: **Age 45** in the US (USPSTF, ACS), continuing to 75. In the UK and much of Europe, organized **FIT programs** typically begin around 50 (England lowered to 50).

en-gastro.q: What are the main screening options and intervals in the US?
en-gastro.a: **Colonoscopy every 10 years**, **FIT annually**, stool DNA-FIT every 1–3 years, **CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years**.

en-gastro.q: Exam trap: a patient has a positive FIT. Can you repeat the FIT to confirm?
en-gastro.a: No. Any positive stool-based test requires **diagnostic colonoscopy**; repeating the stool test is inappropriate.

en-gastro.q: How is screening modified when a first-degree relative had colorectal cancer before age 60?
en-gastro.a: **Colonoscopy every 5 years starting at age 40**, or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, whichever comes first.

en-gastro.q: What is Lynch syndrome and how is it screened?
en-gastro.a: Autosomal dominant **mismatch repair gene** defect (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM) raising colorectal and endometrial cancer risk. **Colonoscopy every 1–2 years** starting around age 20–25.

en-gastro.q: What characterizes familial adenomatous polyposis?
en-gastro.a: Germline **APC mutation** with hundreds to thousands of adenomas and near-100% cancer risk untreated; **prophylactic colectomy** is standard.

en-gastro.q: When should average-risk screening stop?
en-gastro.a: Recommended to **75**; **individualize at 76–85** based on health and prior screening; generally **not recommended after 85**.

en-gastro.q: When is surveillance colonoscopy due after removal of 1–2 tubular adenomas <10 mm?
en-gastro.a: **7–10 years** (US Multi-Society Task Force 2020), assuming a complete, high-quality colonoscopy.

en-gastro.q: How is acute liver failure defined?
en-gastro.a: **Coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) plus hepatic encephalopathy** within **26 weeks** of illness onset in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis.

en-gastro.q: What is the most common cause of acute liver failure in the US and UK, and how is overdose risk assessed?
en-gastro.a: **Acetaminophen (paracetamol)**. For single acute ingestions, plot a level taken **≥4 h** post-ingestion on the nomogram (US line 150 mcg/mL; UK treats at 100 mg/L) and give **N-acetylcysteine**.

en-gastro.q: Is N-acetylcysteine useful in non-acetaminophen acute liver failure?
en-gastro.a: Yes, in **early-grade encephalopathy (grade I–II)** in adults, where it improves transplant-free survival (AASLD).

en-gastro.q: What are the King's College criteria for transplant in acetaminophen-induced ALF?
en-gastro.a: **Arterial pH <7.30** after resuscitation, or all of: **INR >6.5, creatinine >3.4 mg/dL (300 µmol/L), and grade III–IV encephalopathy**.

en-gastro.q: What are the key early management priorities in acute liver failure?
en-gastro.a: **Early transfer to a transplant center**, ICU care, glucose monitoring for hypoglycemia, infection surveillance, and cerebral edema precautions. Avoid correcting INR unless bleeding or before procedures, since it tracks prognosis.

en-gastro.q: How is the R ratio used to classify drug-induced liver injury?
en-gastro.a: **R = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN)**. **R ≥5** hepatocellular, **R ≤2** cholestatic, **2–5** mixed.

en-gastro.q: What is Hy's law?
en-gastro.a: Drug-induced **ALT >3× ULN plus bilirubin >2× ULN** without initial cholestasis or another cause. It predicts about **10% or higher** mortality or transplant risk.

en-gastro.q: Which drug is the most common cause of idiosyncratic DILI in Western series?
en-gastro.a: **Amoxicillin-clavulanate**, typically **cholestatic or mixed** and often delayed, even weeks after stopping. Others: isoniazid, other anti-TB drugs, and herbal/dietary supplements.

en-infecto.q: How does Sepsis-3 define sepsis?
en-infecto.a: Life-threatening **organ dysfunction** caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Organ dysfunction = an acute increase in **SOFA score of ≥2 points**.

en-infecto.q: What are the Sepsis-3 criteria for septic shock?
en-infecto.a: Sepsis needing **vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg** plus **lactate >2 mmol/L** despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Hospital mortality exceeds 40%.

en-infecto.q: What are the qSOFA criteria, and should qSOFA be used alone to screen for sepsis?
en-infecto.a: **RR ≥22/min, altered mentation, SBP ≤100 mmHg** (≥2 = higher risk). Surviving Sepsis 2021 recommends **against qSOFA alone** as a screening tool, compared with SIRS, NEWS, or MEWS.

en-infecto.q: What initial fluid volume does Surviving Sepsis 2021 suggest for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion?
en-infecto.a: At least **30 mL/kg IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours**, preferably **balanced crystalloids** (e.g., lactated Ringer's) over normal saline, then reassess with dynamic measures.

en-infecto.q: What is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock, and what is added next?
en-infecto.a: **Norepinephrine**, targeting an initial **MAP of 65 mmHg**. Add **vasopressin** (usually at norepinephrine 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min) rather than escalating norepinephrine further. Starting peripherally is acceptable to avoid delay.

en-infecto.q: How fast should antibiotics be given in suspected sepsis?
en-infecto.a: Possible shock or high likelihood of sepsis: **within 1 hour**. Possible sepsis without shock: rapid assessment, and antibiotics **within 3 hours** if concern persists. Draw blood cultures first if it causes no significant delay.

en-infecto.q: When are corticosteroids suggested in septic shock?
en-infecto.a: For **ongoing vasopressor need** (norepinephrine ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥4 hours): **IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day**, typically 50 mg IV every 6 hours.

en-infecto.q: Which lactate step belongs to the Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle?
en-infecto.a: Measure lactate at presentation and **remeasure if initial lactate is >2 mmol/L**. Guide resuscitation toward lactate normalization; **capillary refill time** is a useful adjunct.

en-infecto.q: Which commonly used antibiotics reliably cover MRSA?
en-infecto.a: **Vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin, ceftaroline**; oral options for SSTI include **TMP-SMX and doxycycline**. Clindamycin susceptibility is variable, so check local data.

en-infecto.q: Exam trap: why is daptomycin never used for MRSA pneumonia?
en-infecto.a: It is **inactivated by pulmonary surfactant**. Use vancomycin or linezolid instead. Monitor **CK** on daptomycin because of myopathy risk.

en-infecto.q: Which beta-lactams cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
en-infecto.a: **Piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem/imipenem, and aztreonam**. Trap: **ertapenem and ceftriaxone do NOT** cover Pseudomonas. Non-beta-lactam options: ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, aminoglycosides.

en-infecto.q: Which organisms do cephalosporins (e.g., ceftriaxone) miss? Mnemonic?
en-infecto.a: **LAME**: **L**isteria, **A**typicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella), **M**RSA (except ceftaroline), **E**nterococci.

en-infecto.q: What is the treatment of choice for serious ESBL-producing Enterobacterales infection?
en-infecto.a: A **carbapenem** (e.g., meropenem or ertapenem). In the **MERINO trial**, piperacillin-tazobactam was inferior to meropenem for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli/Klebsiella bacteremia.

en-infecto.q: What is an antibiotic 'time-out'?
en-infecto.a: A structured review at **48–72 hours** using culture results and clinical course to **stop, narrow (de-escalate), or switch to oral** therapy, and to set a defined stop date.

en-infecto.q: How is vancomycin dosing monitored under the 2020 IDSA/ASHP consensus?
en-infecto.a: **AUC-guided dosing** (target AUC/MIC **400–600**, assuming MIC 1) is preferred over trough-only monitoring to reduce **nephrotoxicity**, which is increased when combined with piperacillin-tazobactam.

en-infecto.q: What are the major FDA boxed-warning adverse effects of fluoroquinolones?
en-infecto.a: **Tendinitis/tendon rupture**, **peripheral neuropathy**, CNS effects, and myasthenia gravis exacerbation. Also: QT prolongation, dysglycemia, aortic aneurysm/dissection risk, and C. difficile. Avoid for uncomplicated infections when alternatives exist.

en-infecto.q: When should asymptomatic bacteriuria be treated?
en-infecto.a: Only in **pregnancy** and **before urologic procedures breaching the mucosa**. Do not treat it in older adults, diabetics, catheterized patients, or spinal cord injury.

en-infecto.q: What are first-line options for acute uncomplicated cystitis in women (IDSA)?
en-infecto.a: **Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID for 5 days**, **TMP-SMX 160/800 mg PO BID for 3 days** (if local resistance <20%), or **fosfomycin 3 g PO single dose**. **Pivmecillinam** is first-line in Europe.

en-infecto.q: Exam trap: why is nitrofurantoin inappropriate for pyelonephritis?
en-infecto.a: It achieves therapeutic levels **only in the bladder**, not in renal tissue or blood. Also avoid near term pregnancy (neonatal hemolysis) and with significantly reduced CrCl.

en-infecto.q: What is a standard oral regimen for uncomplicated pyelonephritis if fluoroquinolone resistance is low?
en-infecto.a: **Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID for 7 days** or **levofloxacin 750 mg PO daily for 5–7 days**. TMP-SMX for 14 days if the organism is susceptible.

en-infecto.q: How long should an afebrile man with a UTI be treated?
en-infecto.a: **7 days** (a randomized trial showed 7 days non-inferior to 14 days). Consider prostatitis if febrile or recurrent, which needs longer therapy.

en-infecto.q: In catheter-associated UTI, what should be done with a catheter in place >2 weeks?
en-infecto.a: **Replace (or remove) it before obtaining the urine culture**, then treat. Typical duration: **7 days** with prompt response, 10–14 days if response is delayed.

en-infecto.q: Which urinary pathogen causes struvite stones, and why?
en-infecto.a: **Proteus mirabilis**. Its **urease** splits urea into ammonia, alkalinizing urine and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite), often forming staghorn calculi.

en-infecto.q: What is emphysematous pyelonephritis and how is it managed?
en-infecto.a: Gas-forming necrotizing renal infection, mostly in **diabetics**, usually E. coli or Klebsiella. Diagnose with **CT**. Needs IV antibiotics plus **percutaneous drainage** or nephrectomy if severe.

en-infecto.q: How often is the classic meningitis triad present?
en-infecto.a: Fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status occur together in **fewer than half** of adults; nearly all have **at least two of four** when headache is added.

en-infecto.q: Which features warrant CT before lumbar puncture in suspected meningitis (IDSA)?
en-infecto.a: **Immunocompromise, CNS disease history, new seizure, papilledema, abnormal consciousness, focal neurological deficit.** Never delay antibiotics: draw blood cultures and treat before imaging.

en-infecto.q: What is empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis in adults 18–50 years?
en-infecto.a: **Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours** (or cefotaxime). **Age >50 or immunocompromised: add ampicillin** to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

en-infecto.q: How and when is dexamethasone given in suspected bacterial meningitis?
en-infecto.a: **0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 2–4 days**, first dose **10–20 minutes before or with** the first antibiotic. Benefit is mainly in **pneumococcal** meningitis; stop if another cause is confirmed.

en-infecto.q: What is the typical CSF profile in bacterial meningitis?
en-infecto.a: **High opening pressure, neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, low glucose** (CSF:serum ratio ≤0.4), and **high protein**. Viral meningitis: lymphocytes with normal glucose.

en-infecto.q: A patient has fever, confusion, and temporal lobe changes on MRI. What is the empiric treatment?
en-infecto.a: Suspect **HSV encephalitis**: start **IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours** immediately (adjust for renal function) and send CSF HSV PCR.

en-infecto.q: Suspected meningococcal disease with non-blanching rash in UK primary care: what should be done before transfer?
en-infecto.a: Give **parenteral benzylpenicillin** (IM or IV) without delaying urgent hospital transfer. Non-blanching petechiae/purpura with fever signal meningococcal sepsis.

en-infecto.q: What chemoprophylaxis is used for close contacts of meningococcal disease?
en-infecto.a: **Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO once**, **rifampin 600 mg PO every 12 hours for 2 days**, or **ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once** (preferred in pregnancy). Start as soon as possible.

en-infecto.q: Who should be screened for HIV?
en-infecto.a: USPSTF: everyone **aged 15–65 at least once**, younger/older people at increased risk, and **all pregnant people**. CDC recommends opt-out screening at **13–64**. Screen more often with ongoing risk.

en-infecto.q: What is the recommended initial HIV diagnostic test sequence?
en-infecto.a: **4th-generation antigen/antibody (p24 + HIV-1/2 antibody) immunoassay** → if reactive, **HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation immunoassay** → if negative or indeterminate, **HIV-1 RNA (NAT)** to detect acute infection.

en-infecto.q: How does acute HIV infection typically present?
en-infecto.a: A **mononucleosis-like illness** 2–4 weeks after exposure: fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia. Antibody tests may be negative, so order **HIV RNA** if suspected.

en-infecto.q: When should ART be started?
en-infecto.a: In **everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count**, ideally rapidly (same-day possible). Exception: **delay ART 4–6 weeks in cryptococcal meningitis** (and use caution in TB meningitis) because of IRIS-related mortality.

en-infecto.q: What are recommended initial ART regimens for most adults (DHHS)?
en-infecto.a: **INSTI-based**: **bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine**, or **dolutegravir plus TAF or TDF with emtricitabine or lamivudine**. Dolutegravir/lamivudine is an option if no HBV, VL <500,000 copies/mL, and no resistance.

en-infecto.q: At what CD4 counts are PJP and Toxoplasma prophylaxis started?
en-infecto.a: **CD4 <200 cells/µL: TMP-SMX** for Pneumocystis. **CD4 <100 with positive Toxoplasma IgG: TMP-SMX DS daily** covers both. Routine MAC prophylaxis is not needed if ART starts promptly.

en-infecto.q: What are the key rules for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)?
en-infecto.a: Start **within 72 hours** (ideally hours), continue **28 days**, with a **3-drug regimen** (e.g., bictegravir/emtricitabine/TAF or dolutegravir plus TDF/emtricitabine). Test at baseline and follow-up.

en-infecto.q: What must be checked before prescribing abacavir, and why?
en-infecto.a: **HLA-B*57:01** status. Carriers have high risk of a potentially fatal **hypersensitivity reaction**; never rechallenge after a suspected reaction.

en-infecto.q: Which organisms cause purulent versus nonpurulent cellulitis?
en-infecto.a: **Nonpurulent** cellulitis/erysipelas: mainly **beta-hemolytic streptococci**. **Purulent** infections (abscess, furuncle): **Staphylococcus aureus**, including MRSA.

en-infecto.q: What is first-line oral therapy for mild nonpurulent cellulitis?
en-infecto.a: Streptococcal coverage, e.g., **cephalexin 500 mg PO every 6 hours**, dicloxacillin, or penicillin V (clindamycin if allergic), typically for **5 days**, extended if not improving.

en-infecto.q: What is the main treatment for a skin abscess, and when are antibiotics added?
en-infecto.a: **Incision and drainage**. Add MRSA-active antibiotics (TMP-SMX, clindamycin) for systemic signs, large or multiple lesions, immunocompromise, extremes of age, or failed drainage.

en-infecto.q: What are red flags for necrotizing fasciitis?
en-infecto.a: **Pain out of proportion** to findings, rapid spread, tense edema beyond erythema, **bullae, crepitus, skin anesthesia**, and systemic toxicity. Needs **emergency surgical exploration and debridement**.

en-infecto.q: What is empiric antibiotic therapy for necrotizing fasciitis?
en-infecto.a: **Vancomycin (or linezolid) plus piperacillin-tazobactam (or a carbapenem) plus clindamycin**. Clindamycin **suppresses toxin production** in streptococcal and staphylococcal infection.

en-infecto.q: Exam trap: does a low LRINEC score exclude necrotizing fasciitis?
en-infecto.a: **No.** LRINEC has poor sensitivity. Clinical suspicion should prompt **surgical exploration**, which is diagnostic and therapeutic; imaging must not delay surgery.

en-infecto.q: What antibiotic prophylaxis is used for dog, cat, or human bites?
en-infecto.a: **Amoxicillin-clavulanate**, covering **Pasteurella** (dogs, cats), **Eikenella corrodens** (humans), and anaerobes. Cat bites carry high infection risk due to deep puncture wounds.

en-infecto.q: Exam trap: a patient has bilateral red, warm lower legs. Is this likely cellulitis?
en-infecto.a: Usually **not**. Cellulitis is almost always **unilateral**; bilateral erythema suggests **stasis dermatitis**, lipodermatosclerosis, or contact dermatitis. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics.

en-infecto.q: When should C. difficile testing be performed?
en-infecto.a: Only with **≥3 unexplained unformed stools in 24 hours** and no laxative use. Do not test formed stool and do **not** perform a test of cure.

en-infecto.q: What is first-line treatment of an initial C. difficile episode (IDSA/SHEA 2021)?
en-infecto.a: **Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID for 10 days** (preferred) or **vancomycin 125 mg PO QID for 10 days**. Metronidazole only for non-severe disease if these are unavailable.

en-infecto.q: What laboratory values define severe C. difficile infection (IDSA)?
en-infecto.a: **WBC ≥15,000/µL** or **serum creatinine >1.5 mg/dL**. Fulminant disease adds hypotension/shock, ileus, or megacolon.

en-infecto.q: How is fulminant C. difficile infection treated?
en-infecto.a: **Vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG QID** plus **IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours**; add **rectal vancomycin** if ileus. Obtain early **surgical consultation** (colectomy or diverting loop ileostomy).

en-infecto.q: What is an option for C. difficile after multiple recurrences?
en-infecto.a: After **≥2 recurrences**, use **fecal microbiota transplantation or approved microbiota-based products** after a course of standard antibiotics. Fidaxomicin or a vancomycin taper/pulse regimen is used for recurrences.

en-infecto.q: Exam trap: why is alcohol hand rub insufficient for C. difficile?
en-infecto.a: Alcohol **does not kill spores**. Use **soap and water** handwashing, contact precautions, and **sporicidal (bleach-based)** environmental cleaning.

en-infecto.q: What is the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea, and what treats severe cases?
en-infecto.a: **Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)**. For severe diarrhea or dysentery, **azithromycin** is preferred (especially from South/Southeast Asia due to fluoroquinolone resistance).

en-infecto.q: Exam trap: why avoid antibiotics in suspected E. coli O157:H7 (STEC)?
en-infecto.a: Antibiotics may increase Shiga toxin release and **hemolytic uremic syndrome** risk. Suspect it in **bloody diarrhea with little or no fever**; also avoid antimotility agents.

en-infecto.q: How should malaria be excluded in a febrile traveler returning from an endemic area?
en-infecto.a: Treat as **malaria until proven otherwise**. Send **thick and thin blood smears** (plus rapid antigen test) urgently; if negative, repeat **every 12–24 hours for a total of three sets**.

en-infecto.q: Which malaria species is most dangerous, and when does it usually present?
en-infecto.a: **Plasmodium falciparum**. Most cases present **within 1 month** of return and almost all within 3 months; P. vivax/ovale can present months later.

en-infecto.q: Name key features of severe malaria.
en-infecto.a: Impaired consciousness, seizures, prostration, acidosis, hypoglycemia, severe anemia, AKI, jaundice, pulmonary edema, shock, bleeding, or high parasitemia (**WHO >10%; CDC ≥5%**). Any one defines severe malaria.

en-infecto.q: What is the treatment of severe malaria?
en-infecto.a: **IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily**, switching to a full oral ACT course when tolerated. Monitor for **delayed post-artesunate hemolysis**.

en-infecto.q: What treats uncomplicated falciparum malaria?
en-infecto.a: An **artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)**, e.g., **artemether-lumefantrine** taken with fatty food; atovaquone-proguanil is an alternative. Chloroquine resistance is widespread.

en-infecto.q: Why is primaquine or tafenoquine added for P. vivax and P. ovale, and what test is required first?
en-infecto.a: To kill dormant liver **hypnozoites** (radical cure) and prevent relapse. **G6PD testing is required** first because these drugs cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

en-infecto.q: A returning traveler has fever, retro-orbital headache, myalgia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. What analgesic is avoided?
en-infecto.a: Suspect **dengue**: avoid **NSAIDs and aspirin** (bleeding risk); use acetaminophen. Watch for warning signs around **defervescence (days 3–7)**, when plasma leakage peaks.

en-infecto.q: What are classic features of enteric (typhoid) fever?
en-infecto.a: Fever rising stepwise, **relative bradycardia**, abdominal pain, **rose spots**, splenomegaly after travel (especially South Asia). Resistance to fluoroquinolones is common; use **azithromycin** or ceftriaxone/carbapenem for XDR strains.

en-infecto.q: What is first-line treatment for invasive aspergillosis?
en-infecto.a: **Voriconazole** (or **isavuconazole**). Supportive diagnostics: **CT halo sign** in neutropenia and serum/BAL **galactomannan**. Use therapeutic drug monitoring for voriconazole.

en-infecto.q: What are characteristic adverse effects of voriconazole?
en-infecto.a: **Visual disturbances**, hallucinations, **photosensitivity and skin cancer** with long use, **periostitis** (fluoride), hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, and major **CYP450 interactions**.

en-infecto.q: What are risk factors and treatment for mucormycosis?
en-infecto.a: Risks: **DKA**, neutropenia, steroids, **iron overload/deferoxamine**. Black necrotic eschar in rhinocerebral disease. Treat with **liposomal amphotericin B plus urgent surgical debridement**; voriconazole is **inactive**.

en-infecto.q: What is WHO-preferred induction for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis?
en-infecto.a: **Single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg** plus **14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole**. Manage raised ICP with **therapeutic lumbar punctures**; delay ART 4–6 weeks.

en-infecto.q: When are corticosteroids added in HIV-associated Pneumocystis pneumonia?
en-infecto.a: When **PaO2 <70 mmHg** or **A–a gradient ≥35 mmHg** on room air, started with **TMP-SMX**. Typical clues: CD4 <200, hypoxemia, bilateral ground-glass opacities, elevated beta-D-glucan.

en-infecto.q: What are key steps in managing candidemia?
en-infecto.a: **Echinocandin** first-line, **remove central venous catheters**, repeat blood cultures, **dilated eye exam**, and treat **14 days after the first negative culture** with symptom resolution.

en-infecto.q: Exam trap: Candida grows in sputum of a ventilated patient. Treat?
en-infecto.a: **No.** Candida in respiratory secretions almost always reflects **colonization**; Candida pneumonia is very rare. Similarly, asymptomatic candiduria usually needs no treatment unless neutropenic or before urologic procedures.

en-infecto.q: Which Candida species are fluconazole-resistant?
en-infecto.a: **C. krusei** (intrinsically resistant); **C. glabrata** often has reduced susceptibility; **Candida auris** is frequently multidrug-resistant and spreads in healthcare settings. Use an echinocandin empirically.

en-infecto.q: Which vaccines are live and contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression?
en-infecto.a: **MMR, varicella, live attenuated influenza, yellow fever, oral typhoid**. Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is **not live** and is safe in immunocompromise.

en-infecto.q: Who should receive the recombinant zoster vaccine and on what schedule?
en-infecto.a: Adults **≥50 years** and immunocompromised adults **≥19 years**: **2 doses, 2–6 months apart**, regardless of prior shingles or prior live zoster vaccine.

en-infecto.q: What is the adult Tdap schedule, including pregnancy?
en-infecto.a: One Tdap dose if never received, then **Td or Tdap every 10 years**. Give **Tdap in every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks** to protect the newborn from pertussis.

en-infecto.q: What is the current US pneumococcal recommendation for adults?
en-infecto.a: Since 2024, CDC recommends vaccination for all adults **≥50** and at-risk adults **19–49**: **PCV20 or PCV21 alone**, or **PCV15 followed by PPSV23**. UK and EU schedules differ.

en-infecto.q: Is egg allergy a contraindication to influenza vaccine?
en-infecto.a: **No.** Any age-appropriate influenza vaccine can be given regardless of egg allergy severity. Annual vaccination is recommended for everyone **≥6 months**.

en-infecto.q: Who should receive tetanus immune globulin after a wound?
en-infecto.a: Patients with a **dirty/tetanus-prone wound** and **unknown or <3 prior tetanus doses**. Give a toxoid booster if last dose was **>5 years** ago (dirty) or **>10 years** (clean).

en-infecto.q: What is the US adult hepatitis B vaccine recommendation?
en-infecto.a: Universal vaccination for adults **19–59 years**; adults **≥60** with risk factors should be vaccinated, and others ≥60 may be vaccinated.

en-infecto.q: Which older adults should receive an RSV vaccine (CDC)?
en-infecto.a: A **single dose** for all adults **≥75** and adults **60–74** at increased risk (e.g., chronic heart/lung disease, immunocompromise). Recommendations are being expanded to younger at-risk adults; check current national schedules.

en-hemato.q: What is the first step in classifying anemia?
en-hemato.a: Use the **MCV**: **microcytic (<80 fL)**, **normocytic (80–100 fL)**, or **macrocytic (>100 fL)**. Then check the **reticulocyte count** to separate underproduction from loss or destruction.

en-hemato.q: What does the reticulocyte production index (RPI) tell you?
en-hemato.a: **RPI >2** suggests an appropriate marrow response (**hemolysis or blood loss**). **RPI <2** indicates a **hypoproliferative** anemia (deficiency, marrow failure, CKD, inflammation).

en-hemato.q: What are the causes of microcytic anemia?
en-hemato.a: Mnemonic **TAILS**: **T**halassemia, **A**nemia of chronic disease, **I**ron deficiency, **L**ead poisoning, **S**ideroblastic anemia. Iron deficiency is by far the most common.

en-hemato.q: What does the Mentzer index suggest?
en-hemato.a: **MCV ÷ RBC count <13** suggests **thalassemia trait**; **>13** suggests **iron deficiency**. It is only a screening clue; confirm with iron studies and hemoglobin electrophoresis.

en-hemato.q: Which laboratory pattern indicates hemolysis?
en-hemato.a: **Raised LDH, raised indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and reticulocytosis**. A **direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test** separates immune from non-immune hemolysis.

en-hemato.q: Anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and neurological signs: what is suspected, and what is urgent treatment?
en-hemato.a: **Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)** (ADAMTS13 <10%). Start **plasma exchange plus corticosteroids** (with caplacizumab) **without waiting** for ADAMTS13 results; avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding.

en-hemato.q: How do you distinguish vitamin B12 from folate deficiency?
en-hemato.a: Both raise **homocysteine**; only **B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid** and causes **neurological signs** (subacute combined degeneration). Giving folate alone may correct anemia while neuropathy progresses.

en-hemato.q: What causes non-megaloblastic macrocytosis?
en-hemato.a: **Alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic syndrome, reticulocytosis**, and drugs (e.g., hydroxyurea, methotrexate, zidovudine).

en-hemato.q: What is the single most useful test for iron deficiency?
en-hemato.a: **Serum ferritin**; **<30 ng/mL** confirms iron deficiency (AGA uses **<45 ng/mL** in anemic adults). Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may be falsely normal in inflammation.

en-hemato.q: How do iron studies differ between iron deficiency and anemia of chronic disease?
en-hemato.a: **Iron deficiency**: low ferritin, **high TIBC**, low TSAT. **Anemia of chronic disease**: normal/high ferritin, **low TIBC**, low TSAT (hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration).

en-hemato.q: A 62-year-old man has new iron deficiency anemia. What evaluation is mandatory?
en-hemato.a: **Bidirectional endoscopy** (gastroscopy and colonoscopy) to exclude GI malignancy, plus **celiac serology**. Applies to men and postmenopausal women with unexplained iron deficiency.

en-hemato.q: How should oral iron be dosed for best absorption?
en-hemato.a: E.g., **ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental iron) PO once daily or on alternate days**. Higher/multiple daily doses raise **hepcidin** and reduce fractional absorption and tolerance.

en-hemato.q: What reduces oral iron absorption?
en-hemato.a: **PPIs/antacids, calcium, tea/coffee, H. pylori, celiac disease, bariatric surgery**, and inflammation (hepcidin). Taking it with vitamin C on an empty stomach improves absorption.

en-hemato.q: When is IV iron preferred over oral iron?
en-hemato.a: **Oral intolerance or failure, malabsorption, ongoing blood loss, CKD**, **heart failure with iron deficiency**, IBD, and **second/third trimester** pregnancy when rapid repletion is needed.

en-hemato.q: What is the expected response to iron therapy?
en-hemato.a: **Reticulocytosis within 7–10 days** and Hb rise of about **2 g/dL within 3–4 weeks**. Continue ~**3 months after Hb normalizes** to replete stores.

en-hemato.q: Exam trap: which electrolyte abnormality is linked to ferric carboxymaltose?
en-hemato.a: **Hypophosphatemia** (FGF23-mediated renal phosphate wasting), which can be severe or cause osteomalacia with repeated doses. Check phosphate if symptomatic or repeatedly dosed.

en-hemato.q: How is D-dimer used in suspected DVT/PE?
en-hemato.a: Use only when pretest probability (Wells) is **low or intermediate**; a negative result excludes VTE. For age >50, use an **age-adjusted cutoff (age × 10 µg/L FEU)**.

en-hemato.q: What is first-line anticoagulation for most patients with VTE?
en-hemato.a: A **DOAC** (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) over warfarin. Exceptions include **antiphospholipid syndrome**, severe renal impairment, pregnancy, and some drug interactions.

en-hemato.q: What is the apixaban dosing regimen for acute VTE treatment?
en-hemato.a: **10 mg PO BID for 7 days, then 5 mg PO BID**. Rivaroxaban: **15 mg PO BID for 21 days, then 20 mg daily** with food. Edoxaban and dabigatran need initial parenteral heparin.

en-hemato.q: How long should VTE be anticoagulated?
en-hemato.a: **Provoked by a major transient risk factor** (e.g., surgery): **3 months**. **Unprovoked** or persistent risk: consider **indefinite** therapy if bleeding risk is acceptable, reassessed periodically.

en-hemato.q: What is the treatment of high-risk (massive) PE with hypotension?
en-hemato.a: **Systemic thrombolysis** (e.g., **alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours**) unless contraindicated; alternatives are surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy. Start unfractionated heparin.

en-hemato.q: What anticoagulant is used for cancer-associated VTE?
en-hemato.a: **Apixaban, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban**, or **LMWH**. Use caution with edoxaban/rivaroxaban in **luminal GI or GU cancers** because of higher bleeding risk; LMWH or apixaban may be preferred.

en-hemato.q: Exam trap: which anticoagulant is preferred in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome?
en-hemato.a: **Warfarin** (target INR 2–3). DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, showed **more arterial thrombotic events** in high-risk APS (TRAPS trial).

en-hemato.q: How is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) managed?
en-hemato.a: Suspect with **platelet fall >50% at 5–10 days** of heparin or thrombosis (4Ts score). **Stop all heparin**, start a **non-heparin anticoagulant** (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or DOAC). Avoid warfarin until platelets recover.

en-hemato.q: How does bleeding pattern help distinguish platelet from coagulation factor disorders?
en-hemato.a: **Platelet/von Willebrand**: mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, epistaxis, menorrhagia). **Factor deficiency** (hemophilia): **deep bleeding**—hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, delayed post-surgical bleeding.

en-hemato.q: What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, and how is mild type 1 treated?
en-hemato.a: **Von Willebrand disease**, usually **type 1** (quantitative). **Desmopressin (DDAVP)** releases stored VWF; tranexamic acid helps mucosal bleeding. VWF concentrates for major bleeding or surgery.

en-hemato.q: An isolated prolonged aPTT corrects on 1:1 mixing study. What does this mean?
en-hemato.a: A **factor deficiency** (VIII, IX, XI, or XII). **Failure to correct** indicates an **inhibitor**, such as lupus anticoagulant or an acquired factor VIII inhibitor.

en-hemato.q: What are the key features of hemophilia A and B?
en-hemato.a: **X-linked** deficiency of **factor VIII (A)** or **IX (B)**: **prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelets**. Emicizumab is used for hemophilia A prophylaxis; gene therapies exist for both.

en-hemato.q: When is immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) treated in adults, and with what?
en-hemato.a: Treat with **platelets <30,000/µL** or bleeding. First-line: **corticosteroids**; add **IVIG** when a rapid rise is needed. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion; test for HIV and HCV.

en-hemato.q: What laboratory pattern suggests DIC?
en-hemato.a: **Prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, low platelets, elevated D-dimer**, and schistocytes. Treat the **underlying cause**; transfuse platelets, plasma, or cryoprecipitate only for bleeding or procedures.

en-hemato.q: How is warfarin reversed in major bleeding?
en-hemato.a: **Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC)** plus **vitamin K 5–10 mg IV**. Plasma is second-line when PCC is unavailable (slower, volume load).

en-hemato.q: What reverses dabigatran and factor Xa inhibitors in life-threatening bleeding?
en-hemato.a: **Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV.** **Apixaban/rivaroxaban:** **andexanet alfa** where available or **4F-PCC**. Availability and preference vary by country; follow local protocols.

en-hemato.q: What is the molecular basis of sickle cell disease?
en-hemato.a: A point mutation replacing **glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of beta-globin** (HbS). Deoxygenated HbS **polymerizes**, deforming red cells and causing vaso-occlusion and hemolysis.

en-hemato.q: How is an acute vaso-occlusive pain crisis managed?
en-hemato.a: **Rapid opioid analgesia** (ASH: within 1 hour of arrival), reassess every 30–60 minutes, **IV fluids only if hypovolemic**, and incentive spirometry. Routine transfusion is not indicated.

en-hemato.q: What defines acute chest syndrome and how is it treated?
en-hemato.a: **New pulmonary infiltrate plus** fever, chest pain, or respiratory symptoms. Treat with **antibiotics (ceftriaxone plus azithromycin)**, oxygen, incentive spirometry, analgesia, and **transfusion** (exchange if severe).

en-hemato.q: How does hydroxyurea help in sickle cell disease?
en-hemato.a: It **increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF)**, reducing pain crises, acute chest syndrome, transfusions, and mortality. NHLBI recommends offering it to HbSS from **9 months of age**.

en-hemato.q: Why are sickle cell patients at risk of encapsulated organism infection, and what prevents it?
en-hemato.a: **Functional asplenia** (autosplenectomy). Prevent with **penicillin prophylaxis until age 5** and **pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib vaccination**. Fever is an emergency.

en-hemato.q: A child with sickle cell disease has a sudden hemoglobin drop with very low reticulocytes. Likely cause?
en-hemato.a: **Aplastic crisis** from **parvovirus B19**, which infects erythroid precursors. Contrast with **splenic sequestration**: Hb falls with high reticulocytes and an enlarging spleen.

en-hemato.q: How is primary stroke risk screened in children with HbSS?
en-hemato.a: **Transcranial Doppler annually from age 2 to 16**. Velocity **≥200 cm/s** indicates high risk and warrants **chronic transfusion therapy**.

en-hemato.q: Exam trap: why avoid simple transfusion to hemoglobin above 10 g/dL in sickle cell disease?
en-hemato.a: Higher hematocrit increases **blood viscosity** and can worsen vaso-occlusion or cause stroke. Use **exchange transfusion** when HbS must be lowered, e.g., acute stroke.

en-hemato.q: What features point to acute myeloid leukemia (AML)?
en-hemato.a: **Myeloblasts with Auer rods**, myeloperoxidase positive, usually **≥20% blasts** in blood or marrow. WHO 2022/ICC allow lower thresholds with defining genetic abnormalities.

en-hemato.q: Why is acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) a medical emergency?
en-hemato.a: **t(15;17) PML::RARA** causes early **DIC** and hemorrhage. Start **ATRA immediately on suspicion** (with arsenic trioxide) and correct coagulopathy. Watch for **differentiation syndrome**.

en-hemato.q: What defines chronic myeloid leukemia and its first-line therapy?
en-hemato.a: **t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome** forming **BCR::ABL1**. Presents with leukocytosis, **basophilia**, and splenomegaly. Treat with a **tyrosine kinase inhibitor** (e.g., imatinib).

en-hemato.q: What are the diagnostic features of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)?
en-hemato.a: **≥5 × 10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes** co-expressing **CD5 and CD23**; **smudge cells** on smear. Early asymptomatic disease is managed with **watch and wait**.

en-hemato.q: Which autoimmune and late complications are classic in CLL?
en-hemato.a: **Autoimmune hemolytic anemia**, ITP, **hypogammaglobulinemia** with recurrent infections, and **Richter transformation** to aggressive lymphoma (usually DLBCL).

en-hemato.q: What are key facts about acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)?
en-hemato.a: Most common **childhood** cancer; blasts are **TdT positive**. **Philadelphia-positive** ALL is more common in adults and treated with a TKI. Requires **CNS prophylaxis**.

en-hemato.q: What is leukostasis and how is it managed?
en-hemato.a: Symptomatic hyperleukocytosis (often **WBC >100,000/µL** in AML): dyspnea, hypoxia, confusion. Rapid **cytoreduction** (hydroxyurea, induction chemotherapy, ± leukapheresis); **avoid unnecessary RBC transfusion**.

en-hemato.q: What are classic features of hairy cell leukemia?
en-hemato.a: Middle-aged man with **pancytopenia, splenomegaly**, monocytopenia, and a **dry tap**. Cells are **CD11c, CD25, CD103** positive with **BRAF V600E**. Treat with **cladribine**.

en-hemato.q: What is the hallmark cell of classic Hodgkin lymphoma?
en-hemato.a: The **Reed-Sternberg cell**, **CD15+ and CD30+**. Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal age distribution and spreads to **contiguous lymph node groups**.

en-hemato.q: What are lymphoma 'B symptoms'?
en-hemato.a: **Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss >10% in 6 months**. They carry prognostic significance in staging.

en-hemato.q: What is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma and its standard first-line treatment?
en-hemato.a: **Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)**, an aggressive lymphoma. Standard: **R-CHOP**; **pola-R-CHP** is an option for higher-risk disease (IPI ≥2).

en-hemato.q: Which translocation defines follicular lymphoma, and how is low-burden disease managed?
en-hemato.a: **t(14;18)** with **BCL2 overexpression**. It is indolent; asymptomatic low-tumor-burden disease is often managed with **watch and wait**.

en-hemato.q: What are the features of Burkitt lymphoma?
en-hemato.a: **t(8;14) MYC** translocation, **starry-sky** histology, very rapid growth, and high risk of **tumor lysis syndrome**. Requires intensive chemotherapy with TLS prophylaxis.

en-hemato.q: How is lymphoma diagnosed and staged?
en-hemato.a: **Excisional or core biopsy** (fine-needle aspiration is inadequate). Stage with **PET-CT (Lugano classification)**; bone marrow biopsy is usually unnecessary in Hodgkin or DLBCL after PET.

en-hemato.q: What is first-line therapy for localized H. pylori-positive gastric MALT lymphoma?
en-hemato.a: **H. pylori eradication therapy**, which induces remission in most cases. Radiotherapy is used if eradication fails or disease is H. pylori-negative.

en-hemato.q: Which lymphoma is CD5+, CD23−, and cyclin D1 positive?
en-hemato.a: **Mantle cell lymphoma**, due to **t(11;14)** involving CCND1. Contrast with CLL/SLL, which is **CD5+ and CD23+**.

en-hemato.q: What laboratory abnormalities define tumor lysis syndrome, and how is it prevented?
en-hemato.a: **Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia** (± AKI, arrhythmia, seizures). Prevent with **aggressive IV hydration** plus **allopurinol**, or **rasburicase** in high-risk patients.

en-hemato.q: Exam trap: in which patients is rasburicase contraindicated?
en-hemato.a: **G6PD deficiency**: it generates hydrogen peroxide, causing **hemolysis and methemoglobinemia**. Test G6PD in at-risk patients before use.

en-hemato.q: A cancer patient has new back pain and leg weakness. What are the next steps?
en-hemato.a: Suspect **malignant spinal cord compression**: urgent **whole-spine MRI**, **dexamethasone** (commonly 16 mg/day), and definitive **radiotherapy or surgical decompression**. Back pain precedes neurological deficits.

en-hemato.q: How is hypercalcemia of malignancy treated?
en-hemato.a: **IV isotonic saline**, then **zoledronic acid 4 mg IV** (adjust for renal function) or **denosumab** (useful in renal failure). **Calcitonin** gives rapid but short-lived effect. Most cases are PTHrP-mediated.

en-hemato.q: What is the approach to superior vena cava syndrome?
en-hemato.a: Usually due to **lung cancer or lymphoma**. Obtain **tissue diagnosis first** unless there is airway compromise or cerebral edema. **Endovascular stenting** relieves symptoms quickly; avoid empiric steroids before lymphoma biopsy.

en-hemato.q: What causes hyperviscosity syndrome and how is it treated?
en-hemato.a: Most often **Waldenström macroglobulinemia (IgM)** or extreme leukocytosis. Features: visual changes, headache, confusion, mucosal bleeding. Urgent **plasmapheresis** for paraprotein-related cases.

en-hemato.q: How are moderate-to-severe immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicities managed?
en-hemato.a: **Hold the drug** and start **corticosteroids** (e.g., prednisone 1–2 mg/kg/day for grade 3–4). Common targets: colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies. Refractory cases may need infliximab or others.

en-hemato.q: A patient with lung cancer has hypotension, raised JVP, and muffled heart sounds. Diagnosis and treatment?
en-hemato.a: **Malignant pericardial effusion with tamponade** (Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus). Confirm with **echocardiography** and perform urgent **pericardiocentesis**.

en-hemato.q: How does IDSA define febrile neutropenia?
en-hemato.a: **Single oral temperature ≥38.3°C** or **≥38.0°C sustained over 1 hour**, with **ANC <500/µL** or expected to fall below 500/µL within 48 hours.

en-hemato.q: What is the empiric antibiotic of choice in high-risk febrile neutropenia?
en-hemato.a: **Antipseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy** within 60 minutes: **cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem**. Aminoglycosides are added only for instability or suspected resistance.

en-hemato.q: When should vancomycin be added in febrile neutropenia?
en-hemato.a: **Hemodynamic instability, suspected catheter infection, skin/soft tissue infection, pneumonia, MRSA colonization**, or **gram-positive bacteremia**. Not routinely for fever alone.

en-hemato.q: How are low-risk febrile neutropenia patients identified and treated?
en-hemato.a: **MASCC score ≥21** (or CISNE) identifies low risk. Selected patients may receive **oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate** as outpatients with close follow-up.

en-hemato.q: When is empiric antifungal therapy considered in febrile neutropenia?
en-hemato.a: With **persistent fever after 4–7 days** of broad-spectrum antibiotics in high-risk patients expected to remain neutropenic **>7 days**, after evaluation for invasive fungal infection.

en-hemato.q: Exam trap: why can infection be missed in neutropenic patients?
en-hemato.a: Lack of neutrophils **blunts inflammation**: minimal pus, subtle infiltrates, few urinary WBCs. Fever may be the only sign. **Avoid digital rectal exams** and rectal temperatures.

en-hemato.q: When is G-CSF primary prophylaxis recommended?
en-hemato.a: When the chemotherapy regimen has **≥20% risk of febrile neutropenia**, or 10–20% with patient risk factors (e.g., age >65). Routine G-CSF for afebrile neutropenia is not recommended.

en-hemato.q: When can empiric antibiotics be stopped in febrile neutropenia?
en-hemato.a: IDSA traditionally continues until **ANC ≥500/µL and rising**. ECIL allows stopping after **≥72 hours afebrile** and clinically stable, even if still neutropenic. Guidelines differ.

en-hemato.q: What is the restrictive red cell transfusion threshold for most hospitalized adults (AABB 2023)?
en-hemato.a: **Hb <7 g/dL** in hemodynamically stable adults; **7.5 g/dL** for cardiac surgery and **8 g/dL** for orthopedic surgery or preexisting cardiovascular disease. In acute MI, the MINT trial favored a more liberal strategy.

en-hemato.q: How much does one unit of packed red cells raise hemoglobin?
en-hemato.a: About **1 g/dL** (hematocrit **~3%**) in an average adult without ongoing bleeding or hemolysis.

en-hemato.q: What are common platelet transfusion thresholds?
en-hemato.a: **<10,000/µL** for prophylaxis in hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia; **<20,000** before central line; **<50,000** before lumbar puncture or major surgery; higher (~100,000) for neurosurgery.

en-hemato.q: What causes an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction and what are its signs?
en-hemato.a: Usually **ABO incompatibility from clerical error**. Fever, chills, **flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria**, and DIC. **Stop the transfusion**, check identification, and send DAT and hemolysis labs.

en-hemato.q: How do you distinguish TRALI from TACO?
en-hemato.a: **TRALI**: noncardiogenic edema within 6 hours, fever, often **hypotension**, normal BNP. **TACO**: **hypertension**, elevated BNP, volume overload, and **responds to diuretics**.

en-hemato.q: Which patient is at risk of anaphylaxis from blood products?
en-hemato.a: **IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies**. Future transfusions should use **washed** cellular products or **IgA-deficient** plasma.

en-hemato.q: Which patients need irradiated blood components?
en-hemato.a: To prevent **transfusion-associated GVHD**: HSCT recipients, **Hodgkin lymphoma**, purine analogue therapy (e.g., fludarabine), congenital cellular immunodeficiency, and **directed donations from relatives**. Leukoreduction does not prevent TA-GVHD.

en-hemato.q: What are key principles of massive transfusion in trauma?
en-hemato.a: **Balanced ratio (~1:1:1)** of plasma, platelets, and red cells; **tranexamic acid within 3 hours** of injury; monitor and correct **hypocalcemia** (citrate), hypothermia, and acidosis.

en-neuro.q: What is the time window for IV thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke?
en-neuro.a: Within **4.5 hours** of last known well. Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), 10% as bolus and the rest over 60 min; **tenecteplase** single bolus is now an accepted alternative in current guidelines.

en-neuro.q: What is the first imaging study in suspected acute stroke, and why?
en-neuro.a: **Noncontrast head CT** (or MRI) to exclude hemorrhage. Do not delay thrombolysis for other labs; **blood glucose** is the only test required before treatment in most patients.

en-neuro.q: Which common metabolic disturbance must be excluded because it can perfectly mimic a stroke?
en-neuro.a: **Hypoglycemia**. Check capillary glucose immediately in every suspected stroke; focal deficits can resolve completely with glucose.

en-neuro.q: What blood pressure must be reached before and maintained after IV thrombolysis?
en-neuro.a: **<185/110 mmHg** before starting thrombolysis and **<180/105 mmHg** for the first 24 hours afterward.

en-neuro.q: In a patient NOT receiving reperfusion therapy, when should blood pressure be lowered acutely?
en-neuro.a: Only if **>220/120 mmHg** (permissive hypertension); then a cautious reduction of about **15%** in the first 24 hours is reasonable.

en-neuro.q: Who qualifies for mechanical thrombectomy?
en-neuro.a: **Large vessel occlusion** (ICA/proximal MCA) with disabling deficit: within **6 hours**, or **6–24 hours** if imaging shows salvageable tissue (DAWN/DEFUSE-3 criteria). Thrombolysis, if eligible, should not delay it.

en-neuro.q: Name key absolute contraindications to IV thrombolysis.
en-neuro.a: Hemorrhage on CT, active internal bleeding, significant head trauma or intracranial surgery within **3 months**, platelets **<100,000/mm³**, INR **>1.7**, therapeutic LMWH within 24 h, or a DOAC within 48 h (unless labs normal).

en-neuro.q: When should antiplatelets start after an ischemic stroke?
en-neuro.a: Aspirin within **24–48 hours**; if thrombolysed, wait **24 hours** and repeat imaging first. For **minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3)**, short-term aspirin plus clopidogrel for **21 days** is recommended.

en-neuro.q: What is the modern (tissue-based) definition of TIA?
en-neuro.a: A transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia **without acute infarction on imaging**. Symptom duration alone no longer defines it.

en-neuro.q: What are the components of the ABCD2 score?
en-neuro.a: **A**ge ≥60 (1), **B**P ≥140/90 (1), **C**linical: unilateral weakness (2) or speech disturbance alone (1), **D**uration ≥60 min (2) or 10–59 min (1), **D**iabetes (1). Maximum 7.

en-neuro.q: How does UK NICE guidance on TIA triage differ from risk-score-based approaches?
en-neuro.a: NICE (2019) advises **not** using ABCD2 to triage: give **aspirin 300 mg** immediately (unless contraindicated) and arrange specialist assessment **within 24 hours** of symptom onset for all suspected TIAs.

en-neuro.q: When is the risk of stroke after a TIA highest?
en-neuro.a: In the **first 48 hours**, which is why urgent same-day evaluation and early secondary prevention are essential.

en-neuro.q: What antiplatelet regimen is recommended after a high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4)?
en-neuro.a: **Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days** (CHANCE/POINT), then single antiplatelet therapy long term. Longer dual therapy increases bleeding without added benefit.

en-neuro.q: Transient painless monocular vision loss, 'like a curtain coming down.' What is it and what test is urgent?
en-neuro.a: **Amaurosis fugax**, a retinal TIA usually from carotid atheroembolism. Urgent **carotid imaging** (duplex, CTA, or MRA) is required.

en-neuro.q: What degree of symptomatic carotid stenosis warrants endarterectomy, and how soon?
en-neuro.a: Symptomatic **70–99%** stenosis (and selected 50–69%) should undergo carotid endarterectomy ideally **within 2 weeks** of the event.

en-neuro.q: Exam trap: prolonged monitoring after TIA reveals atrial fibrillation. Aspirin or anticoagulation?
en-neuro.a: **Oral anticoagulation** (a DOAC is preferred for nonvalvular AF). Antiplatelets are inferior for cardioembolic prevention.

en-neuro.q: What is the most common cause of spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage and its typical locations?
en-neuro.a: **Chronic hypertension**, typically deep: **basal ganglia (putamen), thalamus, pons, cerebellum**. Recurrent **lobar** hemorrhage in older adults suggests **cerebral amyloid angiopathy**.

en-neuro.q: What is the acute blood pressure target in spontaneous ICH?
en-neuro.a: For SBP 150–220 mmHg, lowering to about **140 mmHg** (range 130–150) is reasonable and safe; avoid dropping SBP **below 130 mmHg** (AHA/ASA 2022).

en-neuro.q: How do you reverse anticoagulation in intracerebral hemorrhage?
en-neuro.a: Warfarin: **4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K**. Dabigatran: **idarucizumab**. Factor Xa inhibitors: **andexanet alfa** or 4-factor PCC. Stop all antithrombotics.

en-neuro.q: Which intracerebral hemorrhage most clearly benefits from surgical evacuation?
en-neuro.a: **Cerebellar hemorrhage** with neurologic deterioration, **brainstem compression**, and/or **hydrocephalus**; evacuate surgically rather than relying on ventricular drain alone.

en-neuro.q: Sudden 'worst headache of my life' peaking within a minute. What is the diagnostic approach?
en-neuro.a: Suspect **subarachnoid hemorrhage**. **Noncontrast CT** is nearly 100% sensitive within **6 hours** of onset; if later or negative with high suspicion, perform **lumbar puncture** (≥12 h after onset) for xanthochromia.

en-neuro.q: What is the most common cause of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage?
en-neuro.a: Rupture of a **saccular (berry) aneurysm**, often at the circle of Willis. Associations include **ADPKD**, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, smoking, and hypertension.

en-neuro.q: Which drug improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH, and at what dose?
en-neuro.a: **Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days**; it reduces delayed cerebral ischemia and poor outcomes. Watch for hypotension.

en-neuro.q: List the major complications of aneurysmal SAH and their typical timing.
en-neuro.a: **Rebleeding** (highest in first 24 h, so secure the aneurysm early), **vasospasm/delayed cerebral ischemia** (days **3–14**), **hydrocephalus**, seizures, and **hyponatremia** (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting).

en-neuro.q: What is the operational definition of convulsive status epilepticus?
en-neuro.a: Seizure activity lasting **≥5 minutes**, or **two or more seizures without full recovery** of consciousness between them. Treat at 5 minutes; do not wait for 30.

en-neuro.q: What is first-line treatment for status epilepticus in adults?
en-neuro.a: A **benzodiazepine**: IV **lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg per dose)**, may repeat once; or **IM midazolam 10 mg** (>40 kg) if no IV access; IV diazepam is an alternative.

en-neuro.q: Which second-line agents are used when status epilepticus persists after benzodiazepines?
en-neuro.a: IV **levetiracetam**, **fosphenytoin**, or **valproate** at loading doses; the ESETT trial showed **similar efficacy** among the three.

en-neuro.q: How is refractory status epilepticus managed?
en-neuro.a: Seizures continuing after benzodiazepine and a second-line drug: **intubate** and start an anesthetic infusion (**midazolam, propofol**, or pentobarbital) with **continuous EEG** monitoring in the ICU.

en-neuro.q: What bedside test must never be missed in a seizing patient, and what precedes glucose in alcoholics?
en-neuro.a: **Capillary glucose**. In malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients, give **IV thiamine** with or before glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

en-neuro.q: Features that favor seizure over syncope?
en-neuro.a: **Lateral tongue biting**, prolonged postictal confusion, head turning, tonic-clonic activity >30 s, and cyanosis. Syncope has brief myoclonic jerks with **rapid recovery**.

en-neuro.q: A patient remains comatose 30 minutes after convulsions stop. What must you exclude?
en-neuro.a: **Nonconvulsive status epilepticus**; obtain an **EEG** urgently. Persistent unexplained altered consciousness after a seizure is NCSE until proven otherwise.

en-neuro.q: Exam trap: which antiseizure drug should be avoided in women of childbearing potential?
en-neuro.a: **Valproate**: high risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders. Prefer **levetiracetam or lamotrigine**; valproate only if no alternative with a pregnancy prevention program.

en-neuro.q: List the headache red flags summarized by the SNOOP mnemonic.
en-neuro.a: **S**ystemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, cancer, immunosuppression), **N**eurologic deficits, **O**nset sudden (thunderclap), **O**lder age at onset (>50), **P**attern change, positional or Valsalva-triggered, papilledema, pregnancy.

en-neuro.q: Patient >50 with new headache, jaw claudication, and high ESR. What do you do first?
en-neuro.a: Suspect **giant cell arteritis** and start **high-dose glucocorticoids immediately**, before temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound, to prevent irreversible vision loss.

en-neuro.q: What are the ICHD-3 criteria for migraine without aura?
en-neuro.a: ≥5 attacks lasting **4–72 h** with ≥2 of: unilateral, pulsating, moderate–severe, worsened by routine activity; plus ≥1 of: **nausea/vomiting** or **photophobia and phonophobia**.

en-neuro.q: What is first-line acute treatment for migraine, and a key triptan contraindication?
en-neuro.a: **NSAID or acetaminophen**, then a **triptan** (often with an NSAID) plus an antiemetic if needed. Triptans are contraindicated in **coronary, cerebrovascular, or peripheral vascular disease** and uncontrolled hypertension.

en-neuro.q: Name common first-line migraine preventive drugs.
en-neuro.a: **Propranolol**, **topiramate** (teratogenic), **amitriptyline**, and candesartan. **CGRP monoclonal antibodies** are used after failure of standard preventives.

en-neuro.q: What defines medication overuse headache?
en-neuro.a: Headache ≥15 days/month in a patient with preexisting headache using simple analgesics **≥15 days/month** or triptans, opioids, or combination analgesics **≥10 days/month** for >3 months.

en-neuro.q: Unilateral orbital pain 15–180 minutes with tearing, rhinorrhea, and restlessness. Diagnosis and acute treatment?
en-neuro.a: **Cluster headache**. Acute: **100% oxygen 12–15 L/min** via nonrebreather mask and/or **subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg**. Preventive: **verapamil**.

en-neuro.q: Young obese woman with headache, transient visual obscurations, and papilledema. Diagnosis and workup?
en-neuro.a: **Idiopathic intracranial hypertension**. MRI with **MR venography** (exclude venous sinus thrombosis), then LP showing **raised opening pressure** with normal CSF. Treat with weight loss and **acetazolamide**.

en-neuro.q: What is the typical patient and common presentations of multiple sclerosis?
en-neuro.a: Young adult, often **female, aged 20–40**. Optic neuritis, partial transverse myelitis, brainstem syndromes (INO), sensory symptoms, **Lhermitte sign**, and **Uhthoff phenomenon** (worse with heat).

en-neuro.q: What core principle underlies the McDonald criteria for MS?
en-neuro.a: Demonstrating **dissemination in space and time** of CNS lesions, with no better explanation. CSF-specific **oligoclonal bands** can substitute for dissemination in time.

en-neuro.q: Where are typical MS lesions on MRI?
en-neuro.a: **Periventricular** (ovoid, perpendicular to ventricles: 'Dawson fingers'), **cortical/juxtacortical**, **infratentorial**, and **spinal cord**; gadolinium-enhancing lesions indicate active inflammation.

en-neuro.q: How is an acute disabling MS relapse treated?
en-neuro.a: **High-dose methylprednisolone** (e.g., 500–1000 mg daily for 3–5 days, IV or oral). It speeds recovery but does not change long-term disability. First exclude infection (pseudo-relapse).

en-neuro.q: Painful eye movements and reduced vision with color desaturation in a young woman. Diagnosis and key sign?
en-neuro.a: **Optic neuritis**, with a **relative afferent pupillary defect**. Vision usually recovers over weeks; MRI brain assesses risk of MS.

en-neuro.q: What is internuclear ophthalmoplegia and its localization?
en-neuro.a: Impaired **adduction** of the eye ipsilateral to a **medial longitudinal fasciculus** lesion, with nystagmus of the abducting eye; convergence often preserved. Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests **MS**.

en-neuro.q: What is the major risk of natalizumab therapy and how is it monitored?
en-neuro.a: **Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy** (JC virus). Risk is stratified by **anti-JCV antibody** status, treatment duration, and prior immunosuppression.

en-neuro.q: Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 segments) with severe optic neuritis. What diagnosis must you test for?
en-neuro.a: **Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder**: test **AQP4-IgG** (and MOG-IgG). Some MS drugs (e.g., interferon, natalizumab, fingolimod) can **worsen** NMOSD.

en-neuro.q: What is required for the clinical diagnosis of parkinsonism?
en-neuro.a: **Bradykinesia** plus **rest tremor** and/or **rigidity** (MDS criteria). Postural instability is typically a late feature in Parkinson disease.

en-neuro.q: What is the core pathology of Parkinson disease?
en-neuro.a: Loss of **dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta** with **Lewy bodies** containing alpha-synuclein.

en-neuro.q: Which non-motor features can precede motor symptoms by years?
en-neuro.a: **REM sleep behavior disorder**, **anosmia**, **constipation**, and depression/anxiety.

en-neuro.q: What is the most effective symptomatic drug for Parkinson disease, and its long-term motor complications?
en-neuro.a: **Levodopa** combined with a decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide). Long-term use causes **wearing-off fluctuations** and **dyskinesias**.

en-neuro.q: Name typical adverse effects of dopamine agonists.
en-neuro.a: **Impulse control disorders** (gambling, hypersexuality, shopping), **sudden sleep attacks**, hallucinations, orthostatic hypotension, and leg edema.

en-neuro.q: Which features suggest atypical parkinsonism rather than Parkinson disease?
en-neuro.a: **Early falls** and vertical gaze palsy (PSP), **early severe autonomic failure** or cerebellar signs (MSA), early dementia with hallucinations (DLB), symmetric onset, and **poor levodopa response**.

en-neuro.q: Exam trap: hospitalized PD patient is made nil by mouth and levodopa stopped. What is the risk?
en-neuro.a: **Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome** (NMS-like) and severe akinesia. Never stop abruptly: give doses **on time**, via NG tube, or switch to a **rotigotine patch**.

en-neuro.q: Which antiemetics and antipsychotics should be avoided in Parkinson disease?
en-neuro.a: Avoid **metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol**, and most typical antipsychotics. Use **domperidone** (where available) for nausea and **quetiapine, clozapine**, or pimavanserin for psychosis.

en-neuro.q: How is dementia (major neurocognitive disorder) defined?
en-neuro.a: Acquired, significant decline in **one or more cognitive domains** that **interferes with independence** in daily activities, not explained by delirium or another mental disorder.

en-neuro.q: Which reversible contributors should be screened in new cognitive impairment?
en-neuro.a: **Vitamin B12**, **TSH**, calcium, glucose, CBC, renal and liver function; syphilis/HIV when indicated; **depression**, medications (anticholinergics), and **structural imaging**.

en-neuro.q: How is Alzheimer disease symptomatically treated?
en-neuro.a: **Cholinesterase inhibitors** (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild–moderate disease; **memantine** for moderate–severe disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated.

en-neuro.q: What must be confirmed before anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab), and what is their key risk?
en-neuro.a: **Early symptomatic** Alzheimer disease with **confirmed amyloid pathology** (PET or CSF). Key risk is **ARIA** (edema/microhemorrhage), higher in APOE ε4 homozygotes. Availability and reimbursement vary (e.g., not recommended by NICE).

en-neuro.q: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder. Diagnosis and key drug warning?
en-neuro.a: **Dementia with Lewy bodies**. Patients have **severe sensitivity to antipsychotics** (especially typical ones such as haloperidol), which can be life-threatening.

en-neuro.q: Early disinhibition, apathy, and compulsive behavior with relatively preserved memory in a 58-year-old. Diagnosis?
en-neuro.a: **Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia**; onset often **before 65**, with frontal and anterior temporal atrophy on imaging.

en-neuro.q: What is the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
en-neuro.a: **Gait disturbance** (magnetic, broad-based), **urinary incontinence**, and **cognitive decline**, with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy. Improvement after **high-volume LP** predicts shunt response.

en-neuro.q: How do you distinguish delirium from dementia at the bedside?
en-neuro.a: Delirium has **acute onset**, **fluctuating course**, and **impaired attention** (use the CAM or 4AT). Dementia is gradual with preserved attention early; delirium frequently complicates dementia.

en-neuro.q: What is the classic presentation of Guillain–Barré syndrome?
en-neuro.a: Rapidly progressive, **symmetric ascending weakness** with **areflexia**, often 1–4 weeks after infection (**Campylobacter jejuni**); nadir within **4 weeks**. Sensory symptoms and back pain are common.

en-neuro.q: What is the classic CSF finding in GBS?
en-neuro.a: **Albuminocytologic dissociation**: high protein with normal cell count. It may be **normal in the first week**; marked pleocytosis suggests another diagnosis (e.g., HIV, lymphoma).

en-neuro.q: How do you monitor respiratory function in GBS, and when should you intubate?
en-neuro.a: Serial **FVC and negative inspiratory force** (not SpO2). The '20/30/40 rule': FVC **<20 mL/kg**, NIF weaker than **−30 cmH2O**, expiratory pressure **<40 cmH2O** signals intubation. Watch for autonomic instability.

en-neuro.q: What is the disease-modifying treatment for GBS?
en-neuro.a: **IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days** or **plasma exchange**, equally effective. **Corticosteroids are not effective.**

en-neuro.q: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after a diarrheal illness. Diagnosis and antibody?
en-neuro.a: **Miller Fisher syndrome**, a GBS variant associated with **anti-GQ1b antibodies**.

en-neuro.q: How does CIDP differ from GBS?
en-neuro.a: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy progresses for **more than 8 weeks** and, unlike GBS, **responds to corticosteroids** (as well as IVIG and plasma exchange).

en-neuro.q: What is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy, and the basic screening panel?
en-neuro.a: **Diabetes** (length-dependent 'stocking-glove' sensory neuropathy). Screen **glucose/HbA1c, B12, TSH**, renal function, and **serum protein electrophoresis/immunofixation**; ask about alcohol and drugs.

en-neuro.q: What are first-line drugs for painful diabetic neuropathy?
en-neuro.a: **Duloxetine**, **amitriptyline**, **pregabalin**, or **gabapentin** (NICE: any one, switching if ineffective). Avoid opioids for long-term use.

en-neuro.q: What is the hallmark clinical feature of myasthenia gravis?
en-neuro.a: **Fatigable weakness** worse later in the day: ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and proximal limb weakness. **Reflexes, sensation, and pupils are normal.**

en-neuro.q: Which antibodies are tested in suspected myasthenia gravis?
en-neuro.a: **Acetylcholine receptor antibodies** (≈85% of generalized MG), then **MuSK** and LRP4 if negative. Seronegative cases rely on **single-fiber EMG** (increased jitter) or repetitive nerve stimulation.

en-neuro.q: Which imaging study is mandatory after diagnosing MG, and why?
en-neuro.a: **CT or MRI of the chest** to look for **thymoma** (≈10–15%). **Thymectomy** benefits AChR-positive generalized MG (MGTX trial) and is required for any thymoma.

en-neuro.q: What are the main treatments for myasthenia gravis?
en-neuro.a: Symptomatic **pyridostigmine**; immunotherapy with **corticosteroids** and steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate); refractory disease: complement inhibitors (eculizumab), FcRn blockers (efgartigimod), rituximab (MuSK).

en-neuro.q: How is myasthenic crisis recognized and treated?
en-neuro.a: Respiratory failure or severe bulbar weakness: monitor **FVC/NIF**, admit to ICU, secure airway if needed, and give **IVIG or plasma exchange**; treat triggers such as infection.

en-neuro.q: Name drugs that can precipitate a myasthenic exacerbation.
en-neuro.a: **Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides**, IV **magnesium**, beta-blockers, neuromuscular blockers, and **immune checkpoint inhibitors**; initiation of high-dose steroids can cause transient worsening.

en-neuro.q: Which simple bedside test supports MG in a patient with ptosis?
en-neuro.a: The **ice pack test**: applying ice to the closed eyelid for ~2 minutes improves ptosis in MG, since cold improves neuromuscular transmission.

en-neuro.q: Proximal leg weakness improving with repeated effort, dry mouth, and hyporeflexia in a smoker. Diagnosis?
en-neuro.a: **Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome**: antibodies to **voltage-gated calcium channels**, strongly associated with **small cell lung cancer**. Reflexes and strength improve after brief exercise (facilitation).

en-urgencia.q: What defines high-quality CPR in adults?
en-urgencia.a: Rate **100–120/min**, depth **5–6 cm (2–2.4 in)**, full chest recoil, **minimal interruptions**, and avoiding excessive ventilation; **30:2** compressions to breaths without an advanced airway.

en-urgencia.q: Which rhythms are shockable, and what follows each shock?
en-urgencia.a: **Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia**. Defibrillate promptly (biphasic 120–200 J per manufacturer), then **resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes** without a pulse check.

en-urgencia.q: What is the dose and timing of epinephrine in adult cardiac arrest?
en-urgencia.a: **1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes**. Nonshockable rhythms: give **as soon as possible**. Shockable: after the **second shock** (AHA) or **third shock** (ERC).

en-urgencia.q: Which antiarrhythmic is used in refractory VF/pulseless VT, and at what dose?
en-urgencia.a: **Amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO bolus**, then **150 mg** if persistent; **lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg** is an acceptable alternative.

en-urgencia.q: What are the reversible causes of cardiac arrest (Hs and Ts)?
en-urgencia.a: **Hs**: hypoxia, hypovolemia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo/hyperkalemia, hypothermia. **Ts**: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (pulmonary or coronary).

en-urgencia.q: What is the role of waveform capnography during CPR?
en-urgencia.a: Confirms and monitors **tube placement**, reflects **CPR quality**, and an **abrupt sustained rise in ETCO2** suggests ROSC. With an advanced airway, give **1 breath every 6 seconds** with continuous compressions.

en-urgencia.q: Exam trap: the monitor shows asystole. Should you defibrillate?
en-urgencia.a: **No.** Asystole and PEA are nonshockable: continue CPR, give epinephrine early, and look for reversible causes. Confirm asystole by checking **leads, gain, and pads**.

en-urgencia.q: What are key targets in post-cardiac arrest care?
en-urgencia.a: SpO2 **92–98%**, avoid hypotension (MAP **≥65 mmHg**), **12-lead ECG** with emergent angiography for STEMI, glucose control, and **active fever prevention** in comatose patients; exact temperature targets differ between AHA and ERC.

en-urgencia.q: What is first-line treatment for adult anaphylaxis?
en-urgencia.a: **IM epinephrine 0.5 mg** (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, '1:1000') into the **anterolateral thigh**, repeated **every 5 minutes** if no improvement. Never delay it for antihistamines.

en-urgencia.q: When can anaphylaxis be diagnosed without skin involvement?
en-urgencia.a: When **hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement** develops acutely after exposure to a **known or highly probable allergen** (WAO 2020). Up to 10–20% of cases lack skin signs.

en-urgencia.q: How should a hypotensive patient with anaphylaxis be positioned?
en-urgencia.a: **Supine with legs raised** (pregnant: left lateral). Sit up if breathing is the main problem. Avoid sudden standing, which can cause fatal 'empty ventricle' collapse.

en-urgencia.q: What is the approach to refractory anaphylaxis?
en-urgencia.a: Persistent respiratory or cardiovascular problems after **two IM doses**: start an **IV epinephrine infusion** with expert help and give rapid **IV crystalloid** boluses (e.g., 500–1000 mL in adults).

en-urgencia.q: What is the role of antihistamines and corticosteroids in anaphylaxis?
en-urgencia.a: **Adjuncts only**: antihistamines treat skin symptoms; they do not reverse airway obstruction or shock. Resuscitation Council UK (2021) no longer recommends **routine corticosteroids** in the acute phase.

en-urgencia.q: Patient on a beta-blocker has anaphylaxis unresponsive to epinephrine. Which drug can help?
en-urgencia.a: **IV glucagon**, which increases cardiac contractility independent of beta-receptors. Watch for vomiting and protect the airway.

en-urgencia.q: When should mast cell tryptase be sampled after suspected anaphylaxis?
en-urgencia.a: As soon as possible after resuscitation starts, a second sample ideally within **1–2 hours** (no later than 4 h), and a **baseline** sample at follow-up or after 24 hours.

en-urgencia.q: What must be arranged before discharging a patient after anaphylaxis?
en-urgencia.a: Observation for **biphasic reactions**, prescription of **two epinephrine autoinjectors** with training, a written emergency plan, and **allergy clinic referral**.

en-urgencia.q: What is shock, and which lab marker reflects tissue hypoperfusion?
en-urgencia.a: Circulatory failure causing inadequate cellular oxygen use. **Lactate >2 mmol/L** reflects hypoperfusion; hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg) is common but not required early.

en-urgencia.q: Compare cardiac output, SVR, and filling pressure across the four shock types.
en-urgencia.a: **Hypovolemic**: low CO, high SVR, low filling. **Cardiogenic**: low CO, high SVR, **high** filling. **Distributive**: **high CO, low SVR**. **Obstructive**: low CO, high SVR, high right-sided pressures.

en-urgencia.q: What defines septic shock (Sepsis-3)?
en-urgencia.a: Sepsis needing **vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg** and **lactate >2 mmol/L** despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

en-urgencia.q: What are the initial priorities in septic shock per Surviving Sepsis Campaign?
en-urgencia.a: **Antibiotics within 1 hour**, blood cultures before if no delay, **30 mL/kg crystalloid** (balanced preferred) within 3 h for hypotension or lactate ≥4, and target **MAP ≥65 mmHg**.

en-urgencia.q: What is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock, and what is added next?
en-urgencia.a: **Norepinephrine**. Add **vasopressin** rather than escalating norepinephrine further, and **IV hydrocortisone** if vasopressor requirements persist.

en-urgencia.q: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin after a cervical spine injury. Diagnosis?
en-urgencia.a: **Neurogenic shock** (loss of sympathetic tone). Exclude hemorrhage first, then give fluids, vasopressors, and **atropine** for bradycardia.

en-urgencia.q: What is Beck's triad, and what is the definitive treatment?
en-urgencia.a: **Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds** in cardiac tamponade. Treat with **pericardiocentesis** or surgical drainage; ultrasound confirms.

en-urgencia.q: Exam trap: a trauma patient with 25% blood loss has a normal blood pressure. Is that reassuring?
en-urgencia.a: **No.** Early hemorrhagic shock is compensated; **tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure** come first. Systolic hypotension typically appears only after **>30% blood volume loss** (ATLS class III).

en-urgencia.q: What is the order of the ATLS primary survey?
en-urgencia.a: **A**irway with cervical spine protection, **B**reathing, **C**irculation with hemorrhage control, **D**isability, **E**xposure. Many systems place **catastrophic hemorrhage control first** (<C>ABCDE or xABCDE).

en-urgencia.q: How do you diagnose and treat tension pneumothorax?
en-urgencia.a: **Clinical diagnosis**: do not wait for X-ray. Immediate decompression (needle in the **4th/5th intercostal space, midaxillary line** in adults, or finger thoracostomy), then chest tube.

en-urgencia.q: What chest tube output indicates a massive hemothorax requiring thoracotomy?
en-urgencia.a: **≥1500 mL** immediately, or **200 mL/hour for 2–4 hours**, or persistent transfusion requirement.

en-urgencia.q: What is the dose and timing of tranexamic acid in trauma hemorrhage?
en-urgencia.a: **1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours** of injury, then **1 g over 8 hours** (CRASH-2). Giving it after 3 hours may increase mortality.

en-urgencia.q: What are the principles of damage control resuscitation?
en-urgencia.a: Stop the bleeding, **limit crystalloids**, early **balanced blood products** (≈1:1:1 plasma:platelets:RBC), **permissive hypotension** until hemorrhage control (not in brain injury), and prevent hypothermia and acidosis.

en-urgencia.q: What are the components of the Glasgow Coma Scale, and what score suggests intubation?
en-urgencia.a: **Eye (1–4), Verbal (1–5), Motor (1–6)**; total 3–15. **GCS ≤8** generally indicates the need for a definitive airway.

en-urgencia.q: Which views does the FAST exam include, and what does a positive FAST mean in an unstable patient?
en-urgencia.a: **Pericardial, right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis** (eFAST adds lungs). Positive FAST plus hemodynamic instability indicates **immediate laparotomy**.

en-urgencia.q: How should a suspected unstable pelvic fracture be managed in the primary survey?
en-urgencia.a: Apply a **pelvic binder centered over the greater trochanters** to reduce volume and bleeding; avoid repeated pelvic springing. Consider angioembolization or preperitoneal packing.

en-urgencia.q: How is burn surface area estimated in adults using the rule of nines?
